Below is one example of how you might implement a custom TensorFlow layer that uses a simplified form of Spike-Timing–Dependent Plasticity (STDP). In the human brain the details of STDP are very complex, but a common phenomenological rule is that if a presynaptic spike precedes a postsynaptic spike then the synapse is potentiated (strengthened), and if the order is reversed it is depressed (weakened). One way to capture this is to maintain “traces” (that decay over time) of pre‐ and postsynaptic activity and then update the weights as

  Δw = A₊ · (pre_trace × post_spike) – A₋ · (post_trace × pre_spike)

where A₊ and A₋ are learning (scaling) constants and the “×” is an outer product giving an update per synapse.

The code below is not meant to be a full brain simulation but a proof-of-concept for a TensorFlow layer whose weights are updated online via an STDP-like rule. (Remember that in a lot of spiking neural network simulations the weights are updated outside of the usual gradient descent back-propagation.) You can then “plug” such layers into your overall network.

Note:
 • We assume that the input to this layer is a batch of presynaptic spike signals (for example, binary values where 1 indicates a spike).
 • We maintain a decaying “trace” for both pre– and postsynaptic neurons.
 • The postsynaptic spike is generated using a threshold on the membrane potential.
 • We update the weights at every forward call (time step); in a more sophisticated model you might update the weights on a slower time scale.
 • This example uses a global (or network‐wide averaged) STDP update; if your network is running with batches you may wish to update traces per sample.

Here is one possible implementation:

------------------------------------------------
import tensorflow as tf
import math

class STDPLayer(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, units,
                 A_plus=0.01, A_minus=0.012,
                 tau_pre=20.0, tau_post=20.0,
                 threshold=1.0, dt=1.0,
                 **kwargs):
        """
        Args:
          units: Number of postsynaptic neurons.
          A_plus: Learning rate constant for potentiation.
          A_minus: Learning rate constant for depression.
          tau_pre: Time constant for pre-synaptic trace decay.
          tau_post: Time constant for post-synaptic trace decay.
          threshold: Firing threshold for postsynaptic neuron.
          dt: The discrete time step.
        """
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.units = units
        self.A_plus = A_plus
        self.A_minus = A_minus
        self.tau_pre = tau_pre
        self.tau_post = tau_post
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.dt = dt

    def build(self, input_shape):
        # Assume input_shape = (batch, input_dim)
        self.input_dim = int(input_shape[-1])
        # Create trainable weight matrix between pre and post neurons.
        # Note: Here we set trainable=False because updates come from the STDP rule rather than gradients.
        self.W = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.input_dim, self.units),
            initializer='glorot_uniform',
            trainable=False,
            name="W")
        
        # Initialize pre- and postsynaptic traces (global across the batch).
        self.pre_trace = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.input_dim,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name="pre_trace")
        self.post_trace = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name="post_trace")
        
        super().build(input_shape)

    def call(self, inputs):
        """
        inputs: presynaptic spike activity, assumed to be a binary tensor (batch_size x input_dim)
        """
        # Compute the postsynaptic membrane potential.
        # In a spiking neuron model, often the weighted input is integrated over time.
        potentials = tf.matmul(inputs, self.W)

        # Generate postsynaptic spikes using a threshold.
        # (This is a very simplified spiking mechanism.)
        out_spikes = tf.cast(tf.greater(potentials, self.threshold), tf.float32)

        # Compute decays (using the Euler approximation).
        decay_pre = math.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_pre)
        decay_post = math.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_post)

        # To update the pre and post traces we average over the batch.
        avg_pre_spikes = tf.reduce_mean(inputs, axis=0)   # shape: (input_dim,)
        avg_post_spikes = tf.reduce_mean(out_spikes, axis=0) # shape: (units,)

        # Update the traces.
        # pre_trace(t+1) = pre_trace(t) * decay + current averaged presynaptic spikes
        new_pre_trace = self.pre_trace * decay_pre + avg_pre_spikes
        # post_trace(t+1) = post_trace(t) * decay + current averaged postsynaptic spikes
        new_post_trace = self.post_trace * decay_post + avg_post_spikes

        # Store back the traces.
        self.pre_trace.assign(new_pre_trace)
        self.post_trace.assign(new_post_trace)

        # Now compute the weight update.
        # The STDP rule (for each synapse from pre neuron i to post neuron j) is:
        #   Δw_ij = A_plus * pre_trace[i] * (post_spike[j]) - A_minus * (pre_spike[i]) * post_trace[j]
        # Here, we use the averaged quantities over the batch.
        # Compute outer products to get a matrix of updates.
        dW_plus = self.A_plus * tf.tensordot(new_pre_trace, avg_post_spikes, axes=0)
        dW_minus = self.A_minus * tf.tensordot(avg_pre_spikes, new_post_trace, axes=0)
        dW = dW_plus - dW_minus

        # Update weights. (Optionally clipping can be applied here.)
        self.W.assign_add(dW)

        return out_spikes

# Example usage:
if __name__ == '__main__':

    batch_size = 10
    input_dim = 5
    outs = 3  # number of postsynaptic neurons

To implement Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) in a custom TensorFlow layer that mimics biological neural networks, we'll create a stateful layer that updates synaptic weights based on spike timing correlations. Below is a Python implementation using TensorFlow and Keras.

### Approach
The layer will:
1. **Track Neuron States**: Membrane potential, pre-synaptic traces, and post-synaptic traces.
2. **Integrate-and-Fire Neuron Model**: Compute spikes based on threshold-crossing of membrane potential.
3. **STDP Learning Rule**: Update weights using exponential decay traces for pre- and post-synaptic spikes.

### Solution Code
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Layer

class STDPDense(Layer):
    def __init__(self, units, 
                 a=1.0, b=1.0, 
                 tau_plus=20.0, tau_minus=20.0, 
                 dt=1.0,
                 v_threshold=1.0, 
                 v_reset=0.0, 
                 leakage=1.0,  # 1.0 means no leakage (tau=inf)
                 **kwargs):
        super(STDPDense, self).__init__(**kwargs)
        self.units = units
        self.a = a  # LTP magnitude
        self.b = b  # LTD magnitude
        self.tau_plus = tau_plus  # LTP time constant
        self.tau_minus = tau_minus  # LTD time constant
        self.dt = dt  # Time step duration
        self.v_threshold = v_threshold  # Spiking threshold
        self.v_reset = v_reset  # Membrane reset after spike
        self.leakage = leakage  # Membrane leakage factor (1.0: no leakage)

    def build(self, input_shape):
        input_dim = input_shape[-1]
        self.kernel = self.add_weight(
            shape=(input_dim, self.units),
            initializer='glorot_uniform',
            trainable=True,
            name='kernel'
        )

        # Non-trainable state variables
        self.pre_traces = self.add_weight(
            shape=(input_dim, self.units),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='pre_traces',
            aggregation=tf.VariableAggregation.MEAN
        )

        self.post_traces = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='post_traces',
            aggregation=tf.VariableAggregation.MEAN
        )

        self.membrane_potential = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='membrane_potential',
            aggregation=tf.VariableAggregation.MEAN
        )

        super().build(input_shape)

    def call(self, inputs, training=None):
        # Ensure batch size is 1 for simplicity
        batch_size = tf.shape(inputs)[0]
        assert batch_size == 1, "Current implementation supports batch_size=1"

        inputs = tf.squeeze(inputs, axis=0)  # (input_dim,)

        # Decay traces
        alpha_plus = tf.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_plus)
        alpha_minus = tf.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_minus)

        new_pre_traces = self.pre_traces * alpha_plus + tf.expand_dims(inputs, -1)
        new_post_traces = self.post_traces * alpha_minus

        # Compute synaptic input to membrane
        synaptic_input = tf.linalg.matvec(self.kernel, inputs)

        # Update membrane potential with leakage and spikes
        new_membrane = self.membrane_potential * self.leakage + synaptic_input

        # Generate post-spike
        post_spikes = tf.cast(new_membrane > self.v_threshold, tf.float32)

        # Reset membrane after spike
        new_membrane = new_membrane * (1 - post_spikes) + self.v_reset * post_spikes

        # Update post_traces with current post_spikes
        new_post_traces += post_spikes

        # Compute STDP delta
        ltp = self.a * post_spikes[None, :] * new_pre_traces
        ltd = self.b * tf.expand_dims(inputs, -1) * new_post_traces
        delta_w = ltp - ltd

        # Apply STDP update to weights
        self.kernel.assign_add(delta_w)

        # Update state variables
        self.pre_traces.assign(new_pre_traces)
        self.post_traces.assign(new_post_traces)
        self.membrane_potential.assign(new_membrane)

        # Return spikes with batch dimension
        return post_spikes[None, :]

    def reset_states(self):
        """Reset all state variables to initial values."""
        self.pre_traces.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.pre_traces))
        self.post_traces.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.post_traces))
        self.membrane_potential.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.membrane_potential))
```

### Explanation
1. **Initialization**: The layer initializes weights and state variables (pre- and post-traces, membrane potential).
2. **Stateful Variables**: The layer maintains non-trainable variables to track the state of each synapse and neuron over time.
3. **Call Method**:
   - **Decay Traces**: Pre- and post-trace values are decayed exponentially based on time constants.
   - **Spike Generation**: Membrane potential integrates synaptic input with leakage. Spikes occur when the membrane crosses a threshold.
   - **Weight Update**: STDP adjusts weights using LTP (strengthening) and LTD (weakening) based on spike timing.
4. **Reset States**: A method to reset all state variables between sequences.

### Usage Example

    STDPDense(units=10, a=1.0, b=1.0, tau_plus=20.0, tau_minus=20.0)

- **Batch Size Limitation**: This implementation assumes a batch size of 1. For larger batches, the state variables would need batch dimensions, complicating the code.
- **Neuron Model**: A simple leaky integrate-and-fire model is used. Adjust parameters like `leakage` and `v_threshold` to match desired dynamics.

Implementing Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) in a custom TensorFlow layer requires combining a spiking neuron model with a mechanism to track spike timing and update synaptic weights accordingly. The goal is to mimic the biological principle where synaptic strength changes based on the relative timing of pre- and post-synaptic spikes.

Here's a conceptual outline and a simplified implementation using a trace-based STDP rule, which is a common way to model this phenomenon computationally:

**1. Biological Concept & Model:**

*   **STDP Rule:** If a presynaptic neuron fires shortly before a postsynaptic neuron, the synapse strengthens (LTP). If the presynaptic neuron fires shortly after, the synapse weakens (LTD).
*   **Trace-Based Model:** We maintain exponentially decaying "traces" of pre- and post-synaptic activity.
    *   `pre_trace`: Increases with each presynaptic spike, then decays. Represents recent presynaptic activity.
    *   `post_trace`: Increases with each postsynaptic spike, then decays. Represents recent postsynaptic activity.
*   **Weight Update:**
    *   LTP occurs when a *postsynaptic* spike happens, proportional to the current `pre_trace`: `Δw += η_p * pre_trace * post_spike`
    *   LTD occurs when a *presynaptic* spike happens, proportional to the current `post_trace`: `Δw -= η_m * pre_spike * post_trace`
    (Where `η_p`, `η_m` are learning rates for potentiation and depression).
*   **Neuron Model:** We need a neuron model that generates spikes. A Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model is a common choice. It integrates input current, leaks potential over time, and fires a spike when its membrane potential crosses a threshold, followed by a reset.

**2. Custom TensorFlow Layer Implementation:**

This implementation uses a simple LIF neuron and the trace-based STDP rule. It maintains state variables for membrane potential and traces. For simplicity, it assumes processing one time step at a time and a batch size of 1.

```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Layer
import math

class STDPLIFLayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self, units,
                 tau_mem=10.0,    # Membrane time constant (ms)
                 tau_syn_pre=5.0, # Pre-synaptic trace time constant (ms)
                 tau_syn_post=5.0,# Post-synaptic trace time constant (ms)
                 v_thresh=1.0,    # Firing threshold
                 v_reset=0.0,     # Reset potential
                 eta_plus=0.01,   # LTP learning rate
                 eta_minus=0.01,  # LTD learning rate
                 dt=1.0,          # Simulation time step (ms)
                 **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.units = units
        self.tau_mem = tau_mem
        self.tau_syn_pre = tau_syn_pre
        self.tau_syn_post = tau_syn_post
        self.v_thresh = v_thresh
        self.v_reset = v_reset
        self.eta_plus = eta_plus
        self.eta_minus = eta_minus
        self.dt = dt

        # Calculate decay factors from time constants
        self.mem_decay = math.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_mem)
        self.pre_trace_decay = math.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_syn_pre)
        self.post_trace_decay = math.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_syn_post)

    def build(self, input_shape):
        # input_shape assumed to be (batch_size, input_dim)
        # For simplicity, we'll assert batch_size=1 later,
        # so state variables don't need a batch dimension.
        input_dim = input_shape[-1]

        # Synaptic weights
        self.kernel = self.add_weight(
            shape=(input_dim, self.units),
            initializer='glorot_uniform',
            trainable=False, # Weights updated by STDP rule, not gradients
            name='kernel'
        )

        # State variables (non-trainable)
        # Membrane potential
        self.potential = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='potential'
        )
        # Pre-synaptic traces (one per synapse)
        self.pre_trace = self.add_weight(
            shape=(input_dim, self.units),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='pre_trace'
        )
        # Post-synaptic traces (one per post-synaptic neuron)
        self.post_trace = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='post_trace'
        )
        super().build(input_shape)

    def call(self, inputs):
        # inputs: Presynaptic spikes (batch_size, input_dim), assumed binary (0 or 1)
        # Assert batch_size=1 for this simple implementation
        tf.debugging.assert_equal(tf.shape(inputs)[0], 1,
                                   message="Batch size must be 1 for this layer.")
        # Remove batch dimension
        pre_spikes = tf.squeeze(inputs, axis=0) # Shape: (input_dim,)

        # --- STDP Pre-Synaptic Update (LTD) ---
        # LTD depends on pre_spikes arriving *now* and recent post_trace
        # Shape: (input_dim, units)
        delta_w_ltd = -self.eta_minus * tf.expand_dims(pre_spikes, axis=-1) * self.post_trace

        # --- Update Pre-Synaptic Traces ---
        # Decay previous traces and add effect of current pre-spikes
        # Shape: (input_dim, units)
        new_pre_trace = self.pre_trace * self.pre_trace_decay + tf.expand_dims(pre_spikes, axis=-1)

        # --- Neuron Dynamics (LIF) ---
        # 1. Decay membrane potential
        new_potential = self.potential * self.mem_decay
        # 2. Integrate weighted inputs (current pre_spikes affect potential)
        synaptic_input = tf.linalg.matvec(self.kernel, pre_spikes)
        new_potential += synaptic_input
        # 3. Generate post-synaptic spikes
        post_spikes = tf.cast(new_potential >= self.v_thresh, tf.float32) # Shape: (units,)
        # 4. Reset potential for neurons that spiked
        new_potential = new_potential * (1.0 - post_spikes) + self.v_reset * post_spikes

        # --- STDP Post-Synaptic Update (LTP) ---
        # LTP depends on post_spikes happening *now* and recent pre_trace
        # Shape: (input_dim, units)
        delta_w_ltp = self.eta_plus * self.pre_trace * post_spikes # Uses pre_trace *before* it's updated with current spikes

        # --- Update Post-Synaptic Traces ---
        # Decay previous trace and add effect of current post_spikes
        # Shape: (units,)
        new_post_trace = self.post_trace * self.post_trace_decay + post_spikes

        # --- Apply Weight Updates ---
        self.kernel.assign_add(delta_w_ltd + delta_w_ltp)
        # Optional: Add weight clipping/normalization here if needed

        # --- Update State Variables ---
        self.potential.assign(new_potential)
        self.pre_trace.assign(new_pre_trace)
        self.post_trace.assign(new_post_trace)

        # Return post-synaptic spikes (add batch dimension back)
        return tf.expand_dims(post_spikes, axis=0) # Shape: (1, units)

    def reset_states(self):
        """Resets the state variables of the layer."""
        self.potential.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.potential))
        self.pre_trace.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.pre_trace))
        self.post_trace.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.post_trace))

```

**3. Explanation:**

*   **`__init__`**: Sets up parameters for the LIF neuron (time constant, threshold, reset) and STDP (time constants for traces, learning rates). Decay factors are pre-calculated.
*   **`build`**: Creates the weight matrix (`kernel`), membrane potential (`potential`), and trace variables (`pre_trace`, `post_trace`). Note `trainable=False` for the kernel, as updates are manual via STDP.
*   **`call`**: This method executes one time step:
    *   Calculates the LTD part of the weight update based on incoming spikes and the existing post-synaptic trace.
    *   Updates the pre-synaptic traces based on incoming spikes.
    *   Updates the LIF neuron's membrane potential (decay, integrate input).
    *   Determines which neurons spike based on the threshold.
    *   Resets the potential of spiking neurons.
    *   Calculates the LTP part of the weight update based on the just-generated post-synaptic spikes and the pre-synaptic trace *before* it was updated by the current pre-spikes (this timing detail is important for some STDP rules).
    *   Updates the post-synaptic traces based on the generated spikes.
    *   Applies the combined LTP and LTD changes to the weights.
    *   Updates the state variables (potential, traces) for the next time step.
    *   Returns the generated post-synaptic spikes.
*   **`reset_states`**: Useful for resetting the layer's internal state between different input sequences.

*   **Alignment:** This model captures the core temporal dependency of STDP using traces and integrates it with a basic LIF neuron. This is a common simplification used in computational neuroscience.
*   **Simplifications:** Real STDP is far more complex:
    *   Depends on spike frequency, dendritic location, neuromodulators.
    *   Multiple timescales and forms of plasticity exist.
    *   Neuron models are often more detailed (e.g., conductance-based).
*   **Batching:** This implementation uses `batch_size=1`. Handling batches requires managing states (potential, traces) for each item in the batch, significantly increasing complexity.
*   **Timing Detail:** The exact timing of trace updates vs. weight updates can vary between models. This implementation uses traces from *before* the current spike for the corresponding update component (e.g., `pre_trace` for LTP caused by `post_spike`).

This code provides a foundation. You can extend it by using more sophisticated neuron models, different STDP curves, adding synaptic delays, or exploring ways to handle batch processing efficiently.

To implement Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) in a custom TensorFlow layer that mimics biological neural networks, we'll create a stateful layer that updates synaptic weights based on spike timing correlations. Below is a Python implementation using TensorFlow and Keras.

### Approach
The layer will:
1. **Track Neuron States**: Membrane potential, pre-synaptic traces, and post-synaptic traces.
2. **Integrate-and-Fire Neuron Model**: Compute spikes based on threshold-crossing of membrane potential.
3. **STDP Learning Rule**: Update weights using exponential decay traces for pre- and post-synaptic spikes.

### Solution Code
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Layer

class STDPDense(Layer):
    def __init__(self, units, 
                 a=1.0, b=1.0, 
                 tau_plus=20.0, tau_minus=20.0, 
                 dt=1.0,
                 v_threshold=1.0, 
                 v_reset=0.0, 
                 leakage=1.0,  # 1.0 means no leakage (tau=inf)
                 **kwargs):
        super(STDPDense, self).__init__(**kwargs)
        self.units = units
        self.a = a  # LTP magnitude
        self.b = b  # LTD magnitude
        self.tau_plus = tau_plus  # LTP time constant
        self.tau_minus = tau_minus  # LTD time constant
        self.dt = dt  # Time step duration
        self.v_threshold = v_threshold  # Spiking threshold
        self.v_reset = v_reset  # Membrane reset after spike
        self.leakage = leakage  # Membrane leakage factor (1.0: no leakage)

    def build(self, input_shape):
        input_dim = input_shape[-1]
        self.kernel = self.add_weight(
            shape=(input_dim, self.units),
            initializer='glorot_uniform',
            trainable=True,
            name='kernel'
        )

        # Non-trainable state variables
        self.pre_traces = self.add_weight(
            shape=(input_dim, self.units),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='pre_traces',
            aggregation=tf.VariableAggregation.MEAN
        )

        self.post_traces = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='post_traces',
            aggregation=tf.VariableAggregation.MEAN
        )

        self.membrane_potential = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name='membrane_potential',
            aggregation=tf.VariableAggregation.MEAN
        )

        super().build(input_shape)

    def call(self, inputs, training=None):
        # Ensure batch size is 1 for simplicity
        batch_size = tf.shape(inputs)[0]
        assert batch_size == 1, "Current implementation supports batch_size=1"

        inputs = tf.squeeze(inputs, axis=0)  # (input_dim,)

        # Decay traces
        alpha_plus = tf.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_plus)
        alpha_minus = tf.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_minus)

        new_pre_traces = self.pre_traces * alpha_plus + tf.expand_dims(inputs, -1)
        new_post_traces = self.post_traces * alpha_minus

        # Compute synaptic input to membrane
        synaptic_input = tf.linalg.matvec(self.kernel, inputs)

        # Update membrane potential with leakage and spikes
        new_membrane = self.membrane_potential * self.leakage + synaptic_input

        # Generate post-spike
        post_spikes = tf.cast(new_membrane > self.v_threshold, tf.float32)

        # Reset membrane after spike
        new_membrane = new_membrane * (1 - post_spikes) + self.v_reset * post_spikes

        # Update post_traces with current post_spikes
        new_post_traces += post_spikes

        # Compute STDP delta
        ltp = self.a * post_spikes[None, :] * new_pre_traces
        ltd = self.b * tf.expand_dims(inputs, -1) * new_post_traces
        delta_w = ltp - ltd

        # Apply STDP update to weights
        self.kernel.assign_add(delta_w)

        # Update state variables
        self.pre_traces.assign(new_pre_traces)
        self.post_traces.assign(new_post_traces)
        self.membrane_potential.assign(new_membrane)

        # Return spikes with batch dimension
        return post_spikes[None, :]

    def reset_states(self):
        """Reset all state variables to initial values."""
        self.pre_traces.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.pre_traces))
        self.post_traces.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.post_traces))
        self.membrane_potential.assign(tf.zeros_like(self.membrane_potential))
```

### Explanation
1. **Initialization**: The layer initializes weights and state variables (pre- and post-traces, membrane potential).
2. **Stateful Variables**: The layer maintains non-trainable variables to track the state of each synapse and neuron over time.
3. **Call Method**:
   - **Decay Traces**: Pre- and post-trace values are decayed exponentially based on time constants.
   - **Spike Generation**: Membrane potential integrates synaptic input with leakage. Spikes occur when the membrane crosses a threshold.
   - **Weight Update**: STDP adjusts weights using LTP (strengthening) and LTD (weakening) based on spike timing.
4. **Reset States**: A method to reset all state variables between sequences.

### Usage Example
```python
# Create a model with the custom layer
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    STDPDense(units=10, a=1.0, b=1.0, tau_plus=20.0, tau_minus=20.0)
])

# Simulate a sequence of inputs (batch_size=1)
import numpy as np

# Reset states before each sequence
model.layers[0].reset_states()

# Example input: 5 time steps, 3 input neurons
inputs = np.random.binomial(1, 0.1, (5, 1, 3)).astype(np.float32)

for t_step in range(5):
    input_step = inputs[t_step]
    output = model(input_step)
    print(f"Time step {t_step+1}: Output spikes {output.numpy().flatten()}")
```

### Notes
- **Batch Size Limitation**: This implementation assumes a batch size of 1. For larger batches, the state variables would need batch dimensions, complicating the code.
- **Neuron Model**: A simple leaky integrate-and-fire model is used. Adjust parameters like `leakage` and `v_threshold` to match desired dynamics.
- **Training**: Since STDP is unsupervised, this layer is suitable for scenarios where learning occurs through spike correlations rather than gradients from a loss function.

Below is one example of how you might implement a custom TensorFlow layer that uses a simplified form of Spike-Timing–Dependent Plasticity (STDP). In the human brain the details of STDP are very complex, but a common phenomenological rule is that if a presynaptic spike precedes a postsynaptic spike then the synapse is potentiated (strengthened), and if the order is reversed it is depressed (weakened). One way to capture this is to maintain “traces” (that decay over time) of pre‐ and postsynaptic activity and then update the weights as

  Δw = A₊ · (pre_trace × post_spike) – A₋ · (post_trace × pre_spike)

where A₊ and A₋ are learning (scaling) constants and the “×” is an outer product giving an update per synapse.

The code below is not meant to be a full brain simulation but a proof-of-concept for a TensorFlow layer whose weights are updated online via an STDP-like rule. (Remember that in a lot of spiking neural network simulations the weights are updated outside of the usual gradient descent back-propagation.) You can then “plug” such layers into your overall network.

Note:
 • We assume that the input to this layer is a batch of presynaptic spike signals (for example, binary values where 1 indicates a spike).
 • We maintain a decaying “trace” for both pre– and postsynaptic neurons.
 • The postsynaptic spike is generated using a threshold on the membrane potential.
 • We update the weights at every forward call (time step); in a more sophisticated model you might update the weights on a slower time scale.
 • This example uses a global (or network‐wide averaged) STDP update; if your network is running with batches you may wish to update traces per sample.

Here is one possible implementation:

------------------------------------------------
import tensorflow as tf
import math

class STDPLayer(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, units,
                 A_plus=0.01, A_minus=0.012,
                 tau_pre=20.0, tau_post=20.0,
                 threshold=1.0, dt=1.0,
                 **kwargs):
        """
        Args:
          units: Number of postsynaptic neurons.
          A_plus: Learning rate constant for potentiation.
          A_minus: Learning rate constant for depression.
          tau_pre: Time constant for pre-synaptic trace decay.
          tau_post: Time constant for post-synaptic trace decay.
          threshold: Firing threshold for postsynaptic neuron.
          dt: The discrete time step.
        """
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.units = units
        self.A_plus = A_plus
        self.A_minus = A_minus
        self.tau_pre = tau_pre
        self.tau_post = tau_post
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.dt = dt

    def build(self, input_shape):
        # Assume input_shape = (batch, input_dim)
        self.input_dim = int(input_shape[-1])
        # Create trainable weight matrix between pre and post neurons.
        # Note: Here we set trainable=False because updates come from the STDP rule rather than gradients.
        self.W = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.input_dim, self.units),
            initializer='glorot_uniform',
            trainable=False,
            name="W")
        
        # Initialize pre- and postsynaptic traces (global across the batch).
        self.pre_trace = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.input_dim,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name="pre_trace")
        self.post_trace = self.add_weight(
            shape=(self.units,),
            initializer='zeros',
            trainable=False,
            name="post_trace")
        
        super().build(input_shape)

    def call(self, inputs):
        """
        inputs: presynaptic spike activity, assumed to be a binary tensor (batch_size x input_dim)
        """
        # Compute the postsynaptic membrane potential.
        # In a spiking neuron model, often the weighted input is integrated over time.
        potentials = tf.matmul(inputs, self.W)

        # Generate postsynaptic spikes using a threshold.
        # (This is a very simplified spiking mechanism.)
        out_spikes = tf.cast(tf.greater(potentials, self.threshold), tf.float32)

        # Compute decays (using the Euler approximation).
        decay_pre = math.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_pre)
        decay_post = math.exp(-self.dt / self.tau_post)

        # To update the pre and post traces we average over the batch.
        avg_pre_spikes = tf.reduce_mean(inputs, axis=0)   # shape: (input_dim,)
        avg_post_spikes = tf.reduce_mean(out_spikes, axis=0) # shape: (units,)

        # Update the traces.
        # pre_trace(t+1) = pre_trace(t) * decay + current averaged presynaptic spikes
        new_pre_trace = self.pre_trace * decay_pre + avg_pre_spikes
        # post_trace(t+1) = post_trace(t) * decay + current averaged postsynaptic spikes
        new_post_trace = self.post_trace * decay_post + avg_post_spikes

        # Store back the traces.
        self.pre_trace.assign(new_pre_trace)
        self.post_trace.assign(new_post_trace)

        # Now compute the weight update.
        # The STDP rule (for each synapse from pre neuron i to post neuron j) is:
        #   Δw_ij = A_plus * pre_trace[i] * (post_spike[j]) - A_minus * (pre_spike[i]) * post_trace[j]
        # Here, we use the averaged quantities over the batch.
        # Compute outer products to get a matrix of updates.
        dW_plus = self.A_plus * tf.tensordot(new_pre_trace, avg_post_spikes, axes=0)
        dW_minus = self.A_minus * tf.tensordot(avg_pre_spikes, new_post_trace, axes=0)
        dW = dW_plus - dW_minus

        # Update weights. (Optionally clipping can be applied here.)
        self.W.assign_add(dW)

        return out_spikes

# Example usage:
if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Create some dummy data: a batch of 10 samples with 5 input neurons.
    batch_size = 10
    input_dim = 5
    outs = 3  # number of postsynaptic neurons

    # Generate random binary (spiking) data.
    sample_inputs = tf.cast(tf.random.uniform((batch_size, input_dim)) > 0.8, tf.float32)

    # Instantiate the layer.
    stdp_layer = STDPLayer(units=outs)
    
    # A simple loop to simulate several time steps.
    for t in range(20):
        spikes = stdp_layer(sample_inputs)
        print("Time step", t, "output spikes:\n", spikes.numpy())
------------------------------------------------

A few points to note:
1. This code assumes that you feed it “spiking” data at each time step. In a simulation you might have an outer loop (or a TensorFlow while_loop) that feeds spike trains over many time steps.
2. The STDP update here uses global “traces” that are averaged over the batch. In practice you might want to track these for each neuron or even per connection.
3. We mark the weight variable as non‐trainable so that its update comes solely from our STDP rule rather than the standard gradient descent.
4. The parameters (A_plus, A_minus, tau_pre, tau_post, threshold, dt) are chosen arbitrarily here. Tuning them may be necessary for your specific simulation.

This code is only a starting point. More advanced brain-inspired models might include more detailed neuronal dynamics (such as membrane potential integration, refractory periods, and delay mechanisms) and a different scheme for handling time (for example, using tf.while_loop or integrating with specialized spiking neural network libraries). 

I hope this example gives you a good starting point to build your custom TensorFlow STDP layer!

Okay, let's break this down.

**My Answer to the Prompt:**

The user wants to pivot hierarchical data stored in a PostgreSQL table. For each row (potentially just leaf nodes, or all nodes), we need to display its ancestors' names, organized into columns based on the ancestor's `rank`. If an ancestor at a specific rank doesn't exist for a given row, the value should be `NULL` (interpreted as `nil`).

**Assumptions:**

1.  "Select all rows": This implies we should generate the ancestry view for *every* row in the original table, treating each as a potential "leaf" for the purpose of this query. If only true leaves (nodes with no children) are desired, the query would need an initial filter.
2.  "Ancestor": It's ambiguous whether the node itself counts as its own ancestor at its rank. I will include the node itself in the potential results.
3.  `nil`: In SQL, this corresponds to `NULL`.
4.  `rank`: Assumed to be numeric, but the approach works for other types too.

**Approach:**

1.  **Recursive CTE:** Use a recursive Common Table Expression (CTE) to find all ancestors for each starting node. The CTE should carry the starting node's ID (`leaf_id`) throughout the recursion.
2.  **Pivoting:** Transform the rows of ancestors into columns based on `rank`. Two common methods in PostgreSQL are:
    *   **Conditional Aggregation:** Use `GROUP BY leaf_id` and `MAX(CASE WHEN rank = ... THEN name END)` for each distinct rank. This is simpler if the ranks are known and fixed.
    *   **`crosstab` function:** Use the `crosstab` function from the `tablefunc` extension. This is more suited for dynamic or numerous ranks but requires defining the output columns explicitly or using dynamic SQL.

**Method 1: Conditional Aggregation**

```sql
-- Assume your table is named 'hierarchy'
-- Assume ranks are integers like 1, 2, 3 for this example.

WITH RECURSIVE ancestor_data AS (
  -- Base case: Each node is the starting point (leaf)
  SELECT
    id AS leaf_id, -- The ID of the node whose ancestry we're tracking
    id,            -- Current node's ID
    name,          -- Current node's name
    parent_id,     -- Current node's parent_id
    rank           -- Current node's rank
  FROM
    hierarchy

  UNION ALL

  -- Recursive step: Move up to the parent
  SELECT
    ad.leaf_id,    -- Keep track of the original leaf
    p.id,
    p.name,
    p.parent_id,
    p.rank
  FROM
    ancestor_data ad
  JOIN
    hierarchy p ON ad.parent_id = p.id -- Join current node to its parent
)
SELECT
  leaf_id,
  -- Pivot using MAX and CASE for each potential rank.
  -- Add/remove lines based on the actual distinct ranks in your table.
  MAX(CASE WHEN rank = 1 THEN name END) AS rank_1_name, -- Returns name or NULL (nil)
  MAX(CASE WHEN rank = 2 THEN name END) AS rank_2_name,
  MAX(CASE WHEN rank = 3 THEN name END) AS rank_3_name
  -- Add more columns for other observed ranks as needed
FROM
  ancestor_data
GROUP BY
  leaf_id
ORDER BY
  leaf_id;

-- Note: If the set of ranks is large or unknown beforehand,
-- you would need dynamic SQL to generate the CASE statements.
-- Note 2: To exclude the node itself from the pivoted columns,
-- add `WHERE id <> leaf_id` before the `GROUP BY` clause.
```

**Method 2: `crosstab` function**

```sql
-- Requires the tablefunc extension
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS tablefunc;

-- Assume your table is named 'hierarchy'

WITH RECURSIVE ancestor_data AS (
  -- Base case: Each node is the starting point (leaf)
  SELECT
    id AS leaf_id, id, name, parent_id, rank
  FROM hierarchy
  UNION ALL
  -- Recursive step: Move up to the parent
  SELECT
    ad.leaf_id, p.id, p.name, p.parent_id, p.rank
  FROM ancestor_data ad JOIN hierarchy p ON ad.parent_id = p.id
)
SELECT *
FROM crosstab(
  -- Source query: Must return leaf_id, rank, name, ordered by leaf_id then rank
  $$
    SELECT
      leaf_id,
      rank,
      name
    FROM ancestor_data
    -- Optional filter: WHERE id <> leaf_id
    ORDER BY 1, 2
  $$,
  -- Category query: Must return the distinct ranks in the desired column order
  $$
    SELECT DISTINCT rank FROM hierarchy ORDER BY 1
  $$
) AS pivoted_data (
  -- Output column definition: Must match source query's first column type
  -- and then one column for each rank value returned by the category query.
  -- The names here MUST match the values from the category query.
  -- Example assumes ranks are integers 1, 2, 3 and name is TEXT.
  -- You MUST adjust this list based on your actual ranks and types.
  leaf_id INT,
  "1" TEXT,  -- Use quotes if rank values are not valid SQL identifiers
  "2" TEXT,
  "3" TEXT
);

-- needs to be generated dynamically using procedural code (e.g., PL/pgSQL)
-- or application-level code to build the full query string.

The `StreamingResponse` only starts consuming the generator when the *client* connecting to the FastAPI app requests the data.

The most idiomatic and robust way to handle this with `httpx` and FastAPI is to use `httpx`'s own streaming request mechanism (`client.stream`) and ensure the client context remains open for the duration of the stream processing.

headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_TOKEN"} # Example header
api_input = {"some": "data"} # Example JSON payload

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/proxy-stream") # Assuming this is within a FastAPI route
async def proxy_stream_endpoint():
    # Define the async generator that handles the request and streams the response
    async def stream_generator():
        # Keep the client open for the duration of the streaming
        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            try:
                # Use client.stream() to initiate the request without reading the body yet
                async with client.stream("POST", target_url, headers=headers, json=api_input) as response:
                    # Optional but recommended: Check for non-OK status codes from the target
                    # You might want to handle errors differently, e.g., log them,
                    # return a different status code to *your* client, etc.

                         error_body = await response.aread()
                         raise HTTPException(status_code=response.status_code, detail=f"Upstream error: {error_body.decode()}")

                    # Stream the response chunk by chunk
                    async for chunk in response.aiter_raw():
                        yield chunk

            except httpx.RequestError as e:
                # Handle network errors during the request
                raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail=f"Service unavailable: {str(e)}")
            except HTTPException:
                 # Re-raise HTTPExceptions raised within the try block
                 raise
            except Exception as e:

                # Log the error properly in a real application
                print(f"Unexpected error during streaming: {e}") # Replace with logging
                raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Internal server error during streaming")
            # The client and response contexts are automatically closed here by 'async with'

    # Return the StreamingResponse using the generator
    # Make sure the media_type matches what the target_url actually returns
    return StreamingResponse(stream_generator(), media_type="text/event-stream")

In the analysis stage the script computes publication trends and rankings of top authors. In the “autogen” (automatic generation) stage the script automatically produces a textual report with the insights.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
A bibliometric analyzer that uses a stateflow approach to automatically generate insights.
It loads bibliometric data (e.g., research paper records with publication year,
citations, authors, etc.) from a CSV file, preprocesses it, analyzes publication trends,
plots the results, and then auto-generates a textual report.
"""

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from transitions import Machine
import sys

class BibliometricAnalyzer:
    # Define the states that represent each analysis step.
    states = ['idle', 'loading', 'preprocessing', 'analyzing', 'visualizing', 'generating_report', 'finished']

    def __init__(self, data_path):
        self.data_path = data_path                # CSV file path containing bibliometrics
        self.bibliometrics = None                 # Pandas DataFrame for the data
        self.insights = {}                        # Dictionary to store analysis results and insights

        # Setup the state machine using the transitions library.
        self.machine = Machine(model=self, states=BibliometricAnalyzer.states, initial='idle')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='load_data', source='idle', dest='loading', before='on_load')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='preprocess_data', source='loading', dest='preprocessing', before='on_preprocess')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='analyze', source='preprocessing', dest='analyzing', before='on_analyze')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='visualize', source='analyzing', dest='visualizing', before='on_visualize')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='generate_report', source='visualizing', dest='generating_report', before='on_generate_report')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='finish', source='generating_report', dest='finished', before='on_finish')

    def on_load(self):
        """Load bibliometric data from the CSV file."""
        try:
            self.bibliometrics = pd.read_csv(self.data_path)
            print(f"[LOADING] Data loaded successfully with {len(self.bibliometrics)} records.")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] Failed to load data: {e}")
            sys.exit(1)

    def on_preprocess(self):
        """Preprocess the data: drop missing values and ensure correct types."""
        initial_count = len(self.bibliometrics)
        self.bibliometrics.dropna(inplace=True)
        try:
            # Ensure 'Year' is an integer and 'Citations' is numeric.
            self.bibliometrics['Year'] = self.bibliometrics['Year'].astype(int)
            self.bibliometrics['Citations'] = pd.to_numeric(self.bibliometrics['Citations'])
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] Failed during type conversion: {e}")
            sys.exit(1)
        print(f"[PREPROCESS] Data cleaned: removed {initial_count - len(self.bibliometrics)} incomplete records.")

    def on_analyze(self):
        """Analyze the bibliometric data and auto-generate insights."""
        print("[ANALYZING] Performing analysis...")
        # Compute publication trends per year.
        publications_per_year = self.bibliometrics.groupby('Year').size()
        # Compute total citations per year.
        citations_per_year = self.bibliometrics.groupby('Year')['Citations'].sum()
        # Determine top 10 authors.
        # Assume the CSV has an 'Authors' column with authors separated by commas.
        authors_series = self.bibliometrics['Authors'].str.split(',')
        authors_exploded = authors_series.explode().str.strip()
        top_authors = authors_exploded.value_counts().head(10)

        self.insights['publications_per_year'] = publications_per_year
        self.insights['citations_per_year'] = citations_per_year
        self.insights['top_authors'] = top_authors

        # Print out key insight summaries.
        print("[ANALYZING] Publication trends by year:")
        print(publications_per_year)
        print("[ANALYZING] Top 10 authors:")
        print(top_authors)

    def on_visualize(self):
        """Visualize the insights using Matplotlib."""
        print("[VISUALIZING] Generating plots...")
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

        # Plot publications per year: Bar chart.
        self.insights['publications_per_year'].plot(kind='bar', ax=ax[0])
        ax[0].set_title("Publications Per Year")
        ax[0].set_xlabel("Year")
        ax[0].set_ylabel("Number of Publications")

        # Plot citations per year: Line plot.
        self.insights['citations_per_year'].plot(kind='line', marker='o', ax=ax[1])
        ax[1].set_title("Total Citations Per Year")
        ax[1].set_xlabel("Year")
        ax[1].set_ylabel("Total Citations")

        # Plot top authors: Horizontal bar chart.
        self.insights['top_authors'].plot(kind='barh', ax=ax[2])
        ax[2].set_title("Top 10 Authors")
        ax[2].set_xlabel("Number of Publications")

        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

    def on_generate_report(self):
        """Automatically generate a textual report summarizing the insights (auto-gen report)."""
        print("[REPORT] Generating the bibliometric analysis report...")
        report_text = []
        report_text.append("Bibliometric Analysis Report")
        report_text.append("============================\n")
        report_text.append("1. Publication Trend by Year:")
        report_text.append(self.insights['publications_per_year'].to_string())
        report_text.append("\n2. Total Citations Per Year:")
        report_text.append(self.insights['citations_per_year'].to_string())
        report_text.append("\n3. Top 10 Authors:")
        report_text.append(self.insights['top_authors'].to_string())
        report_text = "\n".join(report_text)

        try:
            with open('bibliometric_report.txt', 'w') as f:
                f.write(report_text)
            print("[REPORT] Report successfully generated as 'bibliometric_report.txt'.")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] Failed to write report: {e}")

    def on_finish(self):
        """Cleanup or final logging."""
        print("[FINISHED] Bibliometric analysis workflow is complete.")

def main():
    # Check for CSV file path argument.
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("Usage: python bibliometric_analyzer.py <path_to_csv_file>")
        sys.exit(1)

    data_path = sys.argv[1]

    # Instantiate the analyzer.
    analyzer = BibliometricAnalyzer(data_path)

    # Execute the stateflow: the transitions will automatically call the before callbacks.
    analyzer.load_data()         # Transitions from 'idle' to 'loading'
    analyzer.preprocess_data()   # 'loading' -> 'preprocessing'
    analyzer.analyze()           # 'preprocessing' -> 'analyzing'
    analyzer.visualize()         # 'analyzing' -> 'visualizing'
    analyzer.generate_report()   # 'visualizing' -> 'generating_report'
    analyzer.finish()            # 'generating_report' -> 'finished'

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Explanation:

1. The BibliometricAnalyzer class defines a series of states from idle, loading, preprocessing, analyzing, visualizing, generating_report, and finished.
2. Each state transition is triggered via a method (e.g., load_data, preprocess_data, etc.). The “before” callbacks (e.g., on_load, on_preprocess, …) implement the functionality.
3. In the analysis stage, the script automatically computes:
    • The number of publications per year.
    • The total number of citations per year.
    • The top 10 authors (assuming the “Authors” column contains comma‐separated names).
4. The visualization stage uses Matplotlib to plot the insights.
5. Finally, the report stage “autogen” creates a text report with the key findings.

To run this script:
  1. Save it as bibliometric_analyzer.py.
  2. Prepare a CSV file (say, research_bibliometrics.csv) with at least the columns: Year, Citations, Authors, etc.
  3. Run:
     python bibliometric_analyzer.py research_bibliometrics.csv

This script is a template that you can extend further—for example, including additional states, more advanced network analyses (e.g., using NetworkX for collaboration networks), or interactive dashboards.

    """Load and preprocess bibliometric data"""
    df = pd.read_csv(file_path)
    # Basic preprocessing steps
    df['year'] = pd.to_datetime(df['year'], errors='coerce')
    df['authors'] = df['authors'].str.lower().str.replace(';', ', ')
    return df

# Analyze data (State 2)
def analyze_data(data):
    """Perform key bibliometric analyses"""
    analysis = {}

    # Co-authorship network analysis
    G = nx.Graph()
    for _, row in data.iterrows():
        authors = row['authors'].split(', ')
        for i in range(len(authors)):
            for j in range(i+1, len(authors)):
                G.add_edge(authors[i], authors[j], weight=row['citations'])
    analysis['co_authors'] = G

    # Citation trends analysis
    citation_trends = data.groupby('year')['citations'].sum()
    analysis['citation_trends'] = citation_trends

    # Top institutions
    top_institutions = data['institution'].value_counts().head(5)
    analysis['top_institutions'] = top_institutions

    return analysis

# Generate insights (State 3)
def generate_insights(analysis):

    assistant = AssistantAgent(
        name="BibliometricAnalyst",
        llm_config={
            "temperature": 0.3,
            "model": "gpt-3.5-turbo"
        }
    )
    
    proxy = UserProxyAgent(name="Researcher")
    
    # Prepare analysis summary for the agent

        f"Top institutions:\n{analysis['top_institutions'].to_string()}"
    )
    
    # Ask agent for insights
    proxy.initiate_chat(
        assistant,
        message=(
            "Analyze this research community's bibliometric data and provide 3 key insights:\n\n"
            f"{summary}\n\n"
            "Focus on collaboration patterns, growth trends, and leading institutions."
        )
    )
    
    return assistant.last_message['content']

# Main execution flow
def main():
    # Load data
    data = load_data('research_papers.csv')
    
    # Perform analysis

    # Generate visualizations

    print("\nGenerated Insights:")
    print("--------------------------------------------------")
    print(insights)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    analysis = {}

    G = nx.Graph()
    for _, row in data.iterrows():
        authors = row['authors'].split(', ')
        for i in range(len(authors)):
            for j in range(i+1, len(authors)):
                G.add_edge(authors[i], authors[j], weight=row['citations'])
    analysis['co_authors'] = G

    # Citation trends analysis
    citation_trends = data.groupby('year')['citations'].sum()
    analysis['citation_trends'] = citation_trends

    return analysis

        }

        message=(
            "Analyze this research community's bibliometric data and provide 3 key insights:\n\n"
            f"{summary}\n\n"
            "Focus on collaboration patterns, growth trends, and leading institutions."
        )
    )
    
    return assistant.last_message['content']

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
A bibliometric analyzer that uses a stateflow approach to automatically generate insights.
It loads bibliometric data (e.g., research paper records with publication year,
citations, authors, etc.) from a CSV file, preprocesses it, analyzes publication trends,
plots the results, and then auto-generates a textual report.
"""

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from transitions import Machine
import sys

class BibliometricAnalyzer:
    # Define the states that represent each analysis step.
    states = ['idle', 'loading', 'preprocessing', 'analyzing', 'visualizing', 'generating_report', 'finished']

    def __init__(self, data_path):
        self.data_path = data_path                # CSV file path containing bibliometrics
        self.bibliometrics = None                 # Pandas DataFrame for the data
        self.insights = {}                        # Dictionary to store analysis results and insights

        # Setup the state machine using the transitions library.
        self.machine = Machine(model=self, states=BibliometricAnalyzer.states, initial='idle')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='load_data', source='idle', dest='loading', before='on_load')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='preprocess_data', source='loading', dest='preprocessing', before='on_preprocess')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='analyze', source='preprocessing', dest='analyzing', before='on_analyze')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='visualize', source='analyzing', dest='visualizing', before='on_visualize')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='generate_report', source='visualizing', dest='generating_report', before='on_generate_report')
        self.machine.add_transition(trigger='finish', source='generating_report', dest='finished', before='on_finish')

    def on_load(self):
        """Load bibliometric data from the CSV file."""
        try:
            self.bibliometrics = pd.read_csv(self.data_path)
            print(f"[LOADING] Data loaded successfully with {len(self.bibliometrics)} records.")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] Failed to load data: {e}")
            sys.exit(1)

    def on_preprocess(self):
        """Preprocess the data: drop missing values and ensure correct types."""
        initial_count = len(self.bibliometrics)
        self.bibliometrics.dropna(inplace=True)
        try:
            # Ensure 'Year' is an integer and 'Citations' is numeric.
            self.bibliometrics['Year'] = self.bibliometrics['Year'].astype(int)
            self.bibliometrics['Citations'] = pd.to_numeric(self.bibliometrics['Citations'])
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[ERROR] Failed during type conversion: {e}")
            sys.exit(1)
        print(f"[PREPROCESS] Data cleaned: removed {initial_count - len(self.bibliometrics)} incomplete records.")

    def on_analyze(self):
        """Analyze the bibliometric data and auto-generate insights."""
        print("[ANALYZING] Performing analysis...")
        # Compute publication trends per year.
        publications_per_year = self.bibliometrics.groupby('Year').size()
        # Compute total citations per year.
        citations_per_year = self.bibliometrics.groupby('Year')['Citations'].sum()
        # Determine top 10 authors.
        # Assume the CSV has an 'Authors' column with authors separated by commas.
        authors_series = self.bibliometrics['Authors'].str.split(',')
        authors_exploded = authors_series.explode().str.strip()
        top_authors = authors_exploded.value_counts().head(10)

        self.insights['publications_per_year'] = publications_per_year
        self.insights['citations_per_year'] = citations_per_year
        self.insights['top_authors'] = top_authors

        # Print out key insight summaries.
        print("[ANALYZING] Publication trends by year:")
        print(publications_per_year)
        print("[ANALYZING] Top 10 authors:")
        print(top_authors)

    def on_visualize(self):
        """Visualize the insights using Matplotlib."""
        print("[VISUALIZING] Generating plots...")
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

        # Plot publications per year: Bar chart.
        self.insights['publications_per_year'].plot(kind='bar', ax=ax[0])
        ax[0].set_title("Publications Per Year")
        ax[0].set_xlabel("Year")
        ax[0].set_ylabel("Number of Publications")

        # Plot citations per year: Line plot.
        self.insights['citations_per_year'].plot(kind='line', marker='o', ax=ax[1])
        ax[1].set_title("Total Citations Per Year")
        ax[1].set_xlabel("Year")
        ax[1].set_ylabel("Total Citations")

        # Plot top authors: Horizontal bar chart.
        self.insights['top_authors'].plot(kind='barh', ax=ax[2])
        ax[2].set_title("Top 10 Authors")
        ax[2].set_xlabel("Number of Publications")

        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

    def on_generate_report(self):
        """Automatically generate a textual report summarizing the insights (auto-gen report)."""
        print("[REPORT] Generating the bibliometric analysis report...")
        report_text = []

Below is an integrated discussion of the extant scholarly literature on innovation orientation, digital transformation, and SME construction firm performance. I have identified several research gaps by reviewing recent studies and outlining limitations and future directions suggested by scholars. Based on these gaps, I propose a theoretical framework that not only examines the direct impact of innovation orientation on digital transformation but also addresses how these affect firm performance through potential mediators (e.g., dynamic capabilities) or moderators (e.g., absorptive capacity). The Resource-Based View (RBV) (Barney, 1991) and Dynamic Capabilities (DC) perspective (Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997) underpin this framework, given that innovation orientation is seen as a strategic resource and capability that drives digital transformation and ultimately improves performance.

──────────────────────────────
1. Research Gaps Identification

Recent empirical research has documented that innovation orientation can influence a firm’s digital capacity (see, for instance, Chen, Liu, & Zhang, 2021). However, there exist several gaps:

a. Context Specificity:  
Although innovation orientation has been studied in various sectors, research on SME construction firms remains scarce. For example, while studies in high-tech industries are abundant (e.g., Kim & Lee, 2020), the construction sector’s unique project-based and risk-laden environment has not been examined in depth (Lim & Ling, 2020). This “context gap” calls for research that documents how innovation orientation drives digital transformation given the resource constraints and market volatility typical of SME construction firms (Stojanovic & Milosevic, 2019).

b. Directionality and Mechanisms:  
Prior literature has often treated digital transformation as a broad outcome without clearly disentangling its antecedents or underlying mechanisms (Bharadwaj et al., 2013). As highlighted by Dubey et al. (2020), “measurement ambiguity in digital transformation has limited our understanding of its drivers and outcomes.” Consequently, there is a need to identify mediators such as dynamic capabilities (loosely defined as the ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure resources) that can explain how innovation orientation translates into digital transformations (Teece et al., 1997).

c. Measurement and Construct Validity:  
While many studies adopt established scales for performance and innovation, few have validated these instruments in the context of SME construction firms. For instance, instruments measuring digital transformation (e.g., Westerman, Bonnet, & McAfee, 2014) require contextual adaptation to reflect industry-specific digital maturity (e.g., automation in construction, Building Information Modelling [BIM] adoption). Lim et al. (2020) note that “failure to adjust scales for niche industry contexts may lead to misrepresentation of firm capabilities.”

d. Missing Moderating Variables:  
Empirical evidence suggests that environmental dynamism and absorptive capacity play moderating roles in innovation-driven change (Zahra & George, 2002). Yet, their inclusion in the relationship between innovation orientation and digital transformation – particularly in SMEs – has received little attention. Future research could test whether high absorptive capacity amplifies the positive impact of innovation orientation on digital transformation, as suggested by the RBV lens (Barney, 1991).

Table 1. Research Gaps in the Literature

│ Research Gap               │ Identified by             │ Main Findings/Observations                               │
├────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

│ (mediating role)           │ Liu, & Zhang (2021)        │ digital transformation; integration of dynamic capabilities   │
│                            │                            │ as potential mediators suggested for future work.           │
├────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Measurement validity       │ Westerman et al. (2014);   │ Existing scales for digital transformation may not account   │
│ in construction context    │ Lim et al. (2020)          │ for industry-specific factors; customization is warranted.  │
├────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Role of moderators like    │ Zahra & George (2002)      │ Environmental uncertainty/absorptive capacity remain         │
│ absorptive capacity        │                            │ underexplored as moderators in the innovation-digital nexus. │
└────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

──────────────────────────────
2. Theoretical Framework and Hypotheses Development

Drawing on these research gaps, the following conceptual framework is proposed. It posits that an SME construction firm’s innovation orientation (IO) positively influences its digital transformation (DT). In turn, DT enhances firm performance (FP). To better understand the mechanism, dynamic capabilities (DC) are introduced as a mediator in the IO → DT relationship, while absorptive capacity (AC) is proposed as a moderator that intensifies the IO → DT link.

Figure 1. Conceptual Framework (described in text):

Innovation Orientation → Digital Transformation → SME Construction Firm Performance  
        │  
     (dynamic Capabilities as mediator)  
        │  
Absorptive Capacity moderates (IO → DT)

Hypotheses and Supporting Literature:

H1: Innovation Orientation Positively Affects Digital Transformation  
  • Rationale: Innovation orientation reflects an organization’s strategic commitment and ability to invest in innovative practices and processes (Lichtenthaler, 2010). From an RBV perspective, innovation is a key strategic resource that enables firms to reconfigure and integrate digital technologies (Barney, 1991; Chen et al., 2021).  
  • Empirical Support: Chen, Liu, and Zhang (2021) found that “innovation-oriented firms tend to adopt digital technologies at a faster pace, leading to a competitive advantage.”  
  • Measurement: The innovation orientation construct can be measured using scales adapted from Hurley and Hult (1998) that assess attitudes toward innovation, investment in R&D, and strategic flexibility.

H2: Digital Transformation Positively Affects SME Construction Firm Performance  
  • Rationale: Digital transformation leads to improved operational processes, enhanced project management, and overall superior firm outcomes. Under the DC perspective, reconfiguring digital resources fosters agility and improved project delivery (Teece et al., 1997; Bharadwaj et al., 2013).  
  • Empirical Support: Westerman et al. (2014) note that “organizations that have embraced digital transformation report significant gains in performance.”  
  • Measurement: Digital transformation can be measured using adapted versions of the scale by Westerman et al. (2014) and further refined to factor in construction-specific technologies such as BIM and construction management software.

H3: Dynamic Capabilities Mediate the Relationship between Innovation Orientation and Digital Transformation  
  • Rationale: Dynamic capabilities enable firms to sense, seize, and reconfigure resources enabling digital transformation (Teece et al., 1997). Innovation orientation, as a driver of new practices, enhances these capabilities to adopt disruptive digital technologies.  
  • Empirical Support: Dubey et al. (2020) suggest that “the development of dynamic capabilities is critical in translating innovative efforts into tangible digital outcomes.”  
  • Measurement: Dynamic capabilities can be measured following scales used in Zahra, Sapienza, and Davidsson (2006).

H4: Absorptive Capacity Moderates the Relationship between Innovation Orientation and Digital Transformation  
  • Rationale: Firms with high absorptive capacity are better positioned to internalize and implement new knowledge, thereby enhancing the effect of innovation orientation on digital transformation (Zahra & George, 2002).  
  • Empirical Support: According to Zahra and George (2002), “absorptive capacity strengthens the conversion of innovation inputs into digital capabilities.”  
  • Measurement: Absorptive capacity is typically measured by assessing a firm’s ability to recognize, assimilate, and exploit external knowledge (Flatten et al., 2011).

H5: Digital Transformation Partially Mediates the Effect of Innovation Orientation (and via Dynamic Capabilities) on SME Construction Firm Performance

On NixOS, you cannot directly modify files in `/nix/store` as it's immutable. The correct approach is to modify the package *build* process itself so that the resulting package in `/nix/store` already includes your desired theme files and modifications. This is typically done using Nix overlays.

Here's a step-by-step guide:

**1. Get the Theme Tarball SHA256 Hash**

Nix needs a SHA256 hash to verify the integrity of downloaded files. Run this command in your terminal:

```bash
nix-prefetch-url https://github.com/joelacus/deluge-web-dark-theme/raw/main/deluge_web_dark_theme.tar.gz
```

Copy the output hash (it will start with `sha256-`). You'll need this in the next step.

**2. Create a Nix Overlay File**

Create a file (e.g., `~/deluge-theme-overlay.nix`) with the following content. Replace `"sha256-YOUR_HASH_HERE"` with the hash you obtained in Step 1.

```nix
# ~/deluge-theme-overlay.nix
self: super: {
  # Override the standard 'deluge' package provided by nixpkgs
  deluge = super.deluge.overrideAttrs (oldAttrs: rec {
    # Optional: Give it a distinct name to identify the modified package
    pname = oldAttrs.pname + "-with-dark-theme";

    # Fetch the theme tarball using the hash for verification
    themeTarball = self.fetchurl {
      url = "https://github.com/joelacus/deluge-web-dark-theme/raw/main/deluge_web_dark_theme.tar.gz";
      # --- IMPORTANT: Replace with the actual hash from step 1 ---
      sha256 = "sha256-YOUR_HASH_HERE";

Below is one “Nix‑only” approach: instead of trying to change files in a read‐only /nix/store, you override (or “patch”) the deluge package so that its built artifacts already contain the theme files and index.html fix. In other words, you “bake in” the dark theme into your deluge package via a Nix overlay.

Below is an example of how you might do it. (Adjust Python version paths and package names as needed.) This example assumes you’re using the deluge 2 derivation from nixpkgs (or pythonPackages.deluge) and that its web UI files end up in a folder like “lib/python3.8/site‑packages/deluge/ui/web/”. You can confirm the real location by inspecting the package output (with nix run or nix-build).

Step 1. Create an overlay file

Create (or add to) an overlay file such as “~/my-overlays/deluge-dark-theme.nix”. For example:

------------------------------------------------------------
# ~/my-overlays/deluge-dark-theme.nix
self: super: {
  # Override (or patch) the deluge derivation.
  # (Adjust the attribute name – it may be “deluge” or “python3.pkgs.deluge”)
  deluge = super.deluge.overrideAttrs (oldAttrs: rec {
  
    # In the postFixup phase we “inject” the dark theme over the default web UI files.
    # (Adjust the paths below based on your deluge’s file layout and Python version.)
    postFixup = (oldAttrs.postFixup or "") + ''
      # Fetch the dark theme tarball (it contains the icons and images)
      mkdir -p theme-tmp
      wget -qO theme.tar.gz \
       https://github.com/joelacus/deluge-web-dark-theme/raw/main/deluge_web_dark_theme.tar.gz
      tar -C theme-tmp -xzf theme.tar.gz
      
      # Replace the icons and images directories inside the installed deluge web UI.
      # (On Debian this would go to /usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/deluge/ui/web/,
      # so in the derivation output we assume something like: )
      cp -r theme-tmp/deluge/ui/web/icons \
           $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/
      cp -r theme-tmp/deluge/ui/web/images \
           $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/
      
      # Edit index.html: insert the meta viewport tag in the <head>.
      # (Here we assume that <head> appears on one line.
      # You might need to adjust the matching pattern.)
      substituteInPlace $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/index.html \
         --replace "<head>" "<head>\n  <meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1, minimum-scale=1, maximum-scale=1\">"
    ''
  });
}
------------------------------------------------------------

Notes:

• We use wget and tar inside postFixup. (If you prefer, you can also use pkgs.fetchurl or pkgs.fetchTarball—but then you have to “copy” its files in the build phase.)
• Adjust “lib/python3.8/site-packages/…” to the correct location in your deluge package output.
• If your deluge derivation is in a different attribute (for example under “python3.pkgs.deluge”), then modify the overlay accordingly.

Step 2. Tell Nix about your overlay

You can add the overlay to your configuration by one of the usual methods. For example, if you manage your overlays via your “~/.config/nixpkgs/overlays” folder, simply put the above file there (or include it in your “default.nix” overlays list). Alternatively, if you’re using NixOS system overlays, add a reference in your /etc/nixos/configuration.nix like:

------------------------------------------------------------
{ pkgs, ... }:
{
  nixpkgs.overlays = [ (import ~/my-overlays/deluge-dark-theme.nix) ];
  # … your other configuration settings …
}
------------------------------------------------------------

Then rebuild your system (nixos-rebuild switch) or update your user profile.

Step 3. Configure deluge’s web.conf

Unlike files in /nix/store you still want to set user‑overridable config. (In your original instructions you modified web.conf.) On NixOS the web UI configuration (for deluge‑web) is typically stored under your user’s~/.config/deluge/ or under the deluge daemon’s configuration directory. You can modify that file manually or via a home-manager module if you’re using home-manager.

For example, create or edit ~/.config/deluge/web.conf so that the theme line reads:

------------------------------------------------------------
{
  ...,
  "theme": "dark"
}
------------------------------------------------------------

Be sure that if you see a backup file (like web.conf~) you update or remove it.

Step 4. Restart deluge‑web

Once rebuilt and installed, restart deluge‑web. (On NixOS you might be running deluge as a service so use “systemctl restart deluge-web.service” or similar.)

────────────────────────────
Why this works

• Since the /nix/store is immutable, you must “patch” a package at build time. Overlays are the Nix way to modify or extend packages.
• The postFixup hook runs after the main installation process but before the derivation is finalized—letting you add extra files (like the dark theme’s icons and images) and tweak bundled files (like index.html).

────────────────────────────
Customizing further

You might want to have more fine‑grained control. For example, if the positioning of the meta tag in index.html changes you could use a different substituteInPlace pattern or even patch the file with a patch file stored in your repository. The general approach remains the same: override the package so that once built it already matches your desired theme configuration.

────────────────────────────
Summary

In NixOS you don’t modify files in /nix/store manually. Instead you override the deluge package derivation with an overlay that, in its build phases, fetches and extracts the dark theme tarball, copies the icons and images into the proper place, and uses substituteInPlace to patch index.html. Your user configuration (web.conf) remains separate and can be updated as usual.

This “everything in Nix” approach means you can reproduce your system configuration on any machine and you don’t have to worry about the store being read‑only.

Happy hacking!

Below is an example of how you might do it. (Adjust Python version paths and package names as needed.) This example assumes you’re using the deluge 2 derivation from nixpkgs (or pythonPackages.deluge) and that its web UI files end up in a folder like “lib/python3.8/site‑packages/deluge/ui/web/”. You can confirm the real location by inspecting the package output (with nix run or nix-build).

Step 1. Create an overlay file

Create (or add to) an overlay file such as “~/my-overlays/deluge-dark-theme.nix”. For example:

------------------------------------------------------------

self: super: {
  # Override (or patch) the deluge derivation.
  # (Adjust the attribute name – it may be “deluge” or “python3.pkgs.deluge”)
  deluge = super.deluge.overrideAttrs (oldAttrs: rec {
  
    # In the postFixup phase we “inject” the dark theme over the default web UI files.
    # (Adjust the paths below based on your deluge’s file layout and Python version.)
    postFixup = (oldAttrs.postFixup or "") + ''
      # Fetch the dark theme tarball (it contains the icons and images)
      mkdir -p theme-tmp
      wget -qO theme.tar.gz \
       https://github.com/joelacus/deluge-web-dark-theme/raw/main/deluge_web_dark_theme.tar.gz
      tar -C theme-tmp -xzf theme.tar.gz
      
      # Replace the icons and images directories inside the installed deluge web UI.
      # (On Debian this would go to /usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/deluge/ui/web/,
      # so in the derivation output we assume something like: )
      cp -r theme-tmp/deluge/ui/web/icons \
           $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/
      cp -r theme-tmp/deluge/ui/web/images \
           $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/
      
      # Edit index.html: insert the meta viewport tag in the <head>.
      # (Here we assume that <head> appears on one line.
      # You might need to adjust the matching pattern.)
      substituteInPlace $out/lib/python3.8/site-packages/deluge/ui/web/index.html \
         --replace "<head>" "<head>\n  <meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1, minimum-scale=1, maximum-scale=1\">"
    ''
  });
}
------------------------------------------------------------

Notes:

• We use wget and tar inside postFixup. (If you prefer, you can also use pkgs.fetchurl or pkgs.fetchTarball—but then you have to “copy” its files in the build phase.)
• Adjust “lib/python3.8/site-packages/…” to the correct location in your deluge package output.
• If your deluge derivation is in a different attribute (for example under “python3.pkgs.deluge”), then modify the overlay accordingly.

Step 2. Tell Nix about your overlay

You can add the overlay to your configuration by one of the usual methods. For example, if you manage your overlays via your “~/.config/nixpkgs/overlays” folder, simply put the above file there (or include it in your “default.nix” overlays list). Alternatively, if you’re using NixOS system overlays, add a reference in your /etc/nixos/configuration.nix like:

------------------------------------------------------------
