```cpp
  // Get Current Real Time
  DateTime now = rtc.now();
  int real_sec = now.second();
  int real_min = now.minute();
  int real_hour = now.hour();

  // Calculate Model Time
  int real_seconds = real_hour * 3600 + real_min * 60 + real_sec;
  int model_seconds = real_seconds * timeRatio;
  int model_hours = model_seconds / 3600 % 24;
  int model_minutes = (model_seconds % 3600) / 60;

  // Update Lights/TVs
  updateLights(model_hours, model_minutes);
  updateTVs(model_hours, model_minutes);

  // Handle Button Inputs
  checkButton1();
  checkButton2();

  // Update OLED Display
  display.clearDisplay();
  display.setCursor(0, 0);
  display.print("Time: ");
  display.print(model_hours);
  display.print(":");
  display.print(model_minutes < 10 ? "0" : "");
  display.println(model_minutes);
  display.println(getCurrentEvent(model_hours, model_minutes));
  display.display();

  // Flicker Effect for TVs
  applyFlicker(LIVING_ROOM_TV, prevFlicker_LR, flickerInterval_LR);
  applyFlicker(BEDROOM_TV, prevFlicker_BR, flickerInterval_BR);

  delay(200); // Refresh interval
}

// Light Control Functions
void updateLights(int h, int m) {
  // Living Room Lights (7 AM - 9 PM)
  digitalWrite(LIVING_ROOM_LIGHTS, (h >= 7 && h < 21) ? HIGH : LOW);

  // Bedroom Lights (7 AM - 10 PM)
  digitalWrite(BEDROOM_LIGHTS, (h >= 7 && h < 22) ? HIGH : LOW);
}

// TV Control Functions
void updateTVs(int h, int m) {
  // Living Room TV (7 PM - Midnight)
  digitalWrite(LIVING_ROOM_TV, (h >= 19) ? HIGH : LOW);

  // Bedroom TV (6-7 AM for news, 10 PM - Midnight or 11 PM if nighttime is toggled)
  bool bedTVOn = false;
  if ((h >= 6 && h < 7) || 
      (h >= 22 && h < 24) || 
      (h == 24 && m < 60)) {
    bedTVOn = true;
  } else if (!nighttimeEnabled && h == 22 && m < 60) {
    bedTVOn = true;
  }
  digitalWrite(BEDROOM_TV, bedTVOn ? HIGH : LOW);
}

// Flicker Effect
void applyFlicker(int pin, unsigned long &prevTime, int &interval) {
  unsigned long currentMillis = millis();
  if (digitalRead(pin) == HIGH) { // Only flicker if TV is scheduled to be on
    if (currentMillis - prevTime >= interval) {
      prevTime = currentMillis;
      // Randomly toggle LED with 10% off chance
      if (random(0, 100) > 10) {
        digitalWrite(pin, HIGH);
      } else {
        digitalWrite(pin, LOW);
      }
      interval = random(50, 200); // Random interval between 50-200ms
    }
  }
}

// Button Handling
void checkButton1() { // Adjust Time Ratio
  if (digitalRead(BUTTON1_PIN) == LOW) {
    delay(200); // Debounce
    if (digitalRead(BUTTON1_PIN) == LOW) {
      timeRatio = (timeRatio % 10) + 1; // Cycle 1-10
      delay(500); // Prevent multiple triggers
    }
  }
}

void checkButton2() { // Toggle Nighttime Duration
  if (digitalRead(BUTTON2_PIN) == LOW) {
    delay(200); // Debounce
    if (digitalRead(BUTTON2_PIN) == LOW) {
      nighttimeEnabled = !nighttimeEnabled;
      delay(500); // Prevent multiple triggers
    }
  }
}

String getCurrentEvent(int h, int m) {
  String event = "None";
  if (h >= 7 && h < 21) {
    event = "Living Room Lights On";
  } else if (h >= 22 && h < 24) {
    event = "Bedroom TV Night Mode";
  } else if (h >= 6 && h < 7) {
    event = "Morning News (Bedroom TV)";
  }
  return event;
}
```

──────────────────────────────

  • A “simulated clock” that starts (for instance at real RTC “morning” time) and advances as:  
   simTime (in seconds) = simulationStartTime + (millis_elapsed * SIMULATION_FACTOR/1000)  
   (mod 86400 to wrap after midnight).

A sample event schedule might be:  

• Bedroom Morning News (simulate tv flicker)  
  – From 06:00 to 07:00 simulated time  
• Living Room Evening Viewing (simulate flickering tv)  
  – From 19:00 to 20:00 simulated time  
• Bedroom Bedtime (lights off in the house but tv on for bedtime)  
  – Normally from 22:00 for 2 hours (i.e. until midnight)  
  – If “night mode off” (the button is pressed, for example) reduce the event to 1 hour

/*
  House Lighting Automation for Model Railroad Houses
  – Uses a DS3231 RTC and an I2C OLED (SSD1306)
  – Simulation speed adjustable (default 6:1 speed-up)
  – Event schedule:
       • Bedroom Morning News (06:00-07:00) – TV flickers
       • Living Room Evening Viewing (19:00-20:00) – TV flickers
       • Bedroom Bedtime (22:00- midnight normally; 1 hour if night mode off)
  – Outputs: Digital pins drive “TV lights” (LEDs or relays)
*/

#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_GFX.h>
#include <Adafruit_SSD1306.h>
#include "RTClib.h"

// OLED display settings
#define SCREEN_WIDTH 128
#define SCREEN_HEIGHT 64
#define OLED_RESET     -1  // Reset pin not used for many OLEDs
Adafruit_SSD1306 display(SCREEN_WIDTH, SCREEN_HEIGHT, &Wire, OLED_RESET);

// RTC
RTC_DS3231 rtc;

// Simulation factor: number of simulated seconds advanced per real second.
unsigned long SIMULATION_FACTOR = 6; // Default is 6:1. Change as desired.

// We'll use "simulation time" in seconds since midnight. 
unsigned long simulationStartTime = 6 * 3600; // e.g. start at 06:00:00 simulated time.
unsigned long simStartMillis = 0;  // Real millis() at start of simulation

// Define event times (in seconds since midnight)
const unsigned long MORNING_START = 6 * 3600;    // 06:00:00
const unsigned long MORNING_END   = 7 * 3600;    // 07:00:00

const unsigned long EVENING_START = 19 * 3600;   // 19:00:00
const unsigned long EVENING_END   = 20 * 3600;   // 20:00:00

const unsigned long NIGHT_START   = 22 * 3600;   // 22:00:00
// If night mode is enabled, use 2 hours; if off, use 1 hour. We'll decide in loop.
const unsigned long NIGHT_DURATION_NORMAL = 2 * 3600; // 2 hours
const unsigned long NIGHT_DURATION_SHORT  = 1 * 3600;  // 1 hour

// Digital pins for outputs
const int LIVINGROOM_TV_PIN = 2;
const int BEDROOM_TV_PIN    = 3;
const int NIGHT_MODE_PIN    = 4;  // digital input: HIGH means night mode enabled (default)

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(LIVINGROOM_TV_PIN, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(BEDROOM_TV_PIN, OUTPUT);
  
  // configure the input for night mode toggle. Activate internal pull-up so button connects to ground.
  pinMode(NIGHT_MODE_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP);
  
  // Initialize I2C
  Wire.begin();
  
  // Initialize RTC
  if (!rtc.begin()) {
    Serial.println("Couldn't find RTC");
    while (1);
  }
  // Uncomment if you need to set your RTC time. (Run once, then re-comment)
  // rtc.adjust(DateTime(F(__DATE__), F(__TIME__)));
  
  // Initialize the OLED display
  if (!display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, 0x3C)) { // Check your OLED I2C address
    Serial.println(F("SSD1306 allocation failed"));
    for(;;);
  }
  display.clearDisplay();
  display.display();
  
  // Record starting real time and set simulation starting time.
  simStartMillis = millis();
  
  Serial.println("House Lighting Automation Initialized");
}

// Utility: Convert seconds since midnight to HH:MM:SS string
String timeToString(unsigned long seconds) {
  unsigned int hh = seconds / 3600;
  unsigned int mm = (seconds % 3600) / 60;
  unsigned int ss = seconds % 60;
  char buf[9];
  sprintf(buf, "%02d:%02d:%02d", hh, mm, ss);
  return String(buf);
}

// Simulate a TV flicker effect: returns HIGH or LOW on a time–varying basis
bool flickerEffect() {
  // Simple flicker: random ON durations and OFF gaps
  // You can adjust the randomness to get a pleasing flicker effect.
  if (random(0, 100) < 80) { // ~80% chance to be on for a short moment
    return true;
  } else {
    return false;
  }
}

void updateDisplay(unsigned long simSec, const char* eventName) {
  display.clearDisplay();
  display.setTextSize(2);
  display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
  display.setCursor(0, 0);
  display.print("Time:");
  display.println(timeToString(simSec));
  display.setTextSize(1);
  display.println();
  display.print("Event:");
  display.println(eventName);
  display.display();
}

void loop() {
  // Calculate simulated time (in seconds since midnight)
  unsigned long realElapsed = millis() - simStartMillis; // in ms
  // Multiply elapsed seconds by simulation factor:
  unsigned long simElapsed = (realElapsed / 1000UL) * SIMULATION_FACTOR;
  unsigned long simTime = (simulationStartTime + simElapsed) % 86400; // wrap at 24h
  
  // Read night mode toggle input. (Since button is wired pull-up, LOW means pressed)
  bool nightModeEnabled = (digitalRead(NIGHT_MODE_PIN) == HIGH);  // HIGH: default mode, bedtime event lasts 2 hours.
  unsigned long nightDuration = nightModeEnabled ? NIGHT_DURATION_NORMAL : NIGHT_DURATION_SHORT;
  
  // Determine event based on simulated time
  const char* currentEvent = "None";
  
  // OFF state for TVs by default:
  digitalWrite(LIVINGROOM_TV_PIN, LOW);
  digitalWrite(BEDROOM_TV_PIN, LOW);
  
  // Bedroom Morning News event (simulate with flicker effect on bedroom tv)
  if ((simTime >= MORNING_START) && (simTime < MORNING_END)) {
    currentEvent = "Morning News";
    // Flicker effect for bedroom TV:
    if (flickerEffect())
      digitalWrite(BEDROOM_TV_PIN, HIGH);
    else
      digitalWrite(BEDROOM_TV_PIN, LOW);
  }
  // Living Room Evening Viewing event (simulate flickering TV)
  else if ((simTime >= EVENING_START) && (simTime < EVENING_END)) {
    currentEvent = "Evening Viewing";
    if (flickerEffect())
      digitalWrite(LIVINGROOM_TV_PIN, HIGH);
    else
      digitalWrite(LIVINGROOM_TV_PIN, LOW);
  }
  // Bedroom Bedtime event – note: “lights off in house” but the bedroom TV stays on.
  else if ((simTime >= NIGHT_START) && (simTime < NIGHT_START + nightDuration)) {
    currentEvent = "Bedtime TV";
    if (flickerEffect())
      digitalWrite(BEDROOM_TV_PIN, HIGH);
    else
      digitalWrite(BEDROOM_TV_PIN, LOW);
  }
  
  // (You can add further events, e.g., turning on other house lights at other times.)
  
  // Update OLED display:
  updateDisplay(simTime, currentEvent);
  
  // For debugging, also print the simulated time to serial occasionally.
  static unsigned long lastPrint = 0;
  if (millis() - lastPrint > 1000) {
    Serial.print("Simulated time: ");
    Serial.print(timeToString(simTime));
    Serial.print("  Event: ");
    Serial.println(currentEvent);
    lastPrint = millis();
  }
  
  delay(100);  // small delay for smooth updating; adjust as necessary.
}

Notes on the Sketch:

• The simulation “clock” starts at 06:00:00 simulated time (simulationStartTime). You can change that or even use the RTC’s current time as the simulation start.
• Each simulated second is advanced SIMULATION_FACTOR times faster than real seconds. (With SIMULATION_FACTOR = 6, one real second equals 6 simulated seconds.)
• The display shows the simulated time and the “current event” label.

STEP 5. Test and Tweak

2. Verify that the OLED displays the sped-up time and event – the serial monitor will also print updates.

This project divides the work into:

```python
@app.route('/patient', methods=['POST'])
def add_patient():
    data = request.get_json()
    new_patient = Patient(
        name=data['name'],
        surname=data['surname'],
        sex=data['sex'],
```
        age=data['age']
    )
    db.session.add(new_patient)
    db.session.commit()
    return jsonify({'message': 'New patient created'}), 201

@app.route('/patient/<int:patient_id>', methods=['GET'])
def get_patient(patient_id):
    patient = Patient.query.get_or_404(patient_id)
    return jsonify({
        'name': patient.name,
        'surname': patient.surname,
        'sex': patient.sex,
        'age': patient.age,
        'last_analysis_average': patient.last_analysis_average
    })

# New route to update the last_analysis_average from analysis services.
@app.route('/patient/<int:patient_id>/update_average', methods=['PUT'])
def update_average(patient_id):
    patient = Patient.query.get_or_404(patient_id)
    data = request.get_json()
    if 'average' in data:
        patient.last_analysis_average = data['average']
        patient.last_saved = datetime.utcnow()
        db.session.commit()
        return jsonify({'message': 'Patient average updated'}), 200
    return jsonify({'error': 'No average provided'}), 400

Okay, let's outline the steps for configuring Meraki devices using the REST API with Python.

**My Answer:**

Here's a step-by-step guide on configuring Meraki network devices (Firewalls, Switches, Access Points, Sensors) using the Meraki REST API, leveraging Python and the official Meraki Python SDK for easier interaction.

**Prerequisites:**

1.  **Meraki Dashboard Account & API Key:**
    *   Log in to your [Meraki Dashboard](https://dashboard.meraki.com).
    *   Navigate to **Organization** > **Settings** > **API access**.
    *   Ensure API access is **Enabled**.
    *   Go to your **Profile** (top-right icon) > **My profile**.
    *   Scroll down to the **API access** section and click **Generate new API key**.
    *   **Important:** Copy the generated key immediately and store it securely. You won't be able to see it again. Treat this key like a password.
2.  **Python Installation:** Ensure you have Python 3.x installed on your system.
3.  **Install Meraki Python SDK:** The SDK simplifies API interactions. Install it using pip:
    ```bash
    pip install meraki
    ```
4.  **Secure API Key Storage:** Avoid hardcoding your API key in scripts. Use environment variables:
    ```bash
    # On Linux/macOS
    export MERAKI_DASHBOARD_API_KEY='YOUR_API_KEY_HERE'

    # On Windows (Command Prompt)
    set MERAKI_DASHBOARD_API_KEY=YOUR_API_KEY_HERE

    # On Windows (PowerShell)
    $env:MERAKI_DASHBOARD_API_KEY='YOUR_API_KEY_HERE'
    ```
    You can also use `.env` files with libraries like `python-dotenv`.

**Step-by-Step Configuration using Python:**

**Step 1: Initialize the Meraki SDK Client**

Create a Python script and import the necessary library. The SDK can automatically pick up the API key from the environment variable `MERAKI_DASHBOARD_API_KEY`.

```python
import meraki
import os
import json

# Initialize the DashboardAPI client
# It automatically looks for 'MERAKI_DASHBOARD_API_KEY' environment variable
# Add suppress_logging=True to reduce console noise from the SDK
dashboard = meraki.DashboardAPI(suppress_logging=True)

# Alternatively, pass the key directly (less secure):
# api_key = 'YOUR_API_KEY_HERE'
# dashboard = meraki.DashboardAPI(api_key, suppress_logging=True)
```

**Step 2: Identify Your Organization and Network IDs**

Most API calls require `organizationId` and/or `networkId`.

```python
try:
    # Get organizations the API key has access to
    organizations = dashboard.organizations.getOrganizations()
    if not organizations:
        print("No organizations found. Check API key permissions.")
        exit()

    # Assuming you want the first organization (adjust if needed)
    organization_id = organizations[0]['id']
    print(f"Using Organization ID: {organization_id}")
    print(f"Organization Name: {organizations[0]['name']}")

    # Get networks within that organization
    networks = dashboard.organizations.getOrganizationNetworks(organization_id)
    if not networks:
        print(f"No networks found in organization {organization_id}.")
        exit()

    # Find a specific network by name (example)
    target_network_name = "Your Network Name" # CHANGE THIS
    network_id = None
    for net in networks:
        print(f"  Network Name: {net['name']}, ID: {net['id']}")
        if net['name'] == target_network_name:
            network_id = net['id']

    if network_id:
        print(f"\nFound Target Network ID: {network_id}")
    else:
        print(f"\nCould not find network named '{target_network_name}'. Please check the name or use a specific ID.")
        # You might want to list networks and prompt the user or use a known ID directly
        # network_id = "L_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" # Hardcode if known and stable
        exit()

except meraki.APIError as e:
    print(f"Meraki API error: {e}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"An error occurred: {e}")
```

**Step 3: Configure Devices (Examples)**

You'll use the `network_id` obtained above. Replace placeholder values with your actual desired configuration.

*   **Firewall (MX) - Update L3 Firewall Rules:**

    *   **Note:** This *replaces* all existing rules. Get the current rules first if you want to append or modify.

    ```python
    try:
        new_rules = {
            "rules": [
                {
                    "comment": "Allow Internal DNS",
                    "policy": "allow",
                    "protocol": "udp",
                    "destPort": "53",
                    "destCidr": "10.0.0.53", # Example internal DNS server
                    "srcCidr": "10.0.0.0/8"   # Example internal network
                },
                {
                    "comment": "Deny Telnet Outbound",
                    "policy": "deny",
                    "protocol": "tcp",
                    "destPort": "23",
                    "destCidr": "Any",
                    "srcCidr": "Any"
                }
                # Add more rules as needed
            ],
            "syslogEnabled": True # Optionally enable syslog for firewall rules
        }

        print(f"\nUpdating L3 Firewall rules for network {network_id}...")
        response = dashboard.appliance.updateNetworkApplianceFirewallL3FirewallRules(
            networkId=network_id,
            updateNetworkApplianceFirewallL3FirewallRules=new_rules # Pass the payload here
        )
        print("L3 Firewall rules updated successfully.")
        # print(json.dumps(response, indent=2)) # Print response if needed

    except meraki.APIError as e:
        print(f"Error updating firewall rules: {e}")
    ```

*   **Switch (MS) - Update Switch Port Configuration:**

    *   You need the switch's `serial` number and the `portId` (usually the port number as a string).

    ```python
    switch_serial = "Qxxx-xxxx-xxxx" # CHANGE THIS to your switch serial
    port_id = "5"                   # CHANGE THIS to the target port number

    try:
        port_config = {
            "name": "Uplink Port",
            "enabled": True,
            "type": "trunk", # 'access' or 'trunk'
            "vlan": 1,       # Native VLAN for trunk, or Access VLAN
            "allowedVlans": "1,10,20", # Allowed VLANs for trunk
            "poeEnabled": False,
            "stpGuard": "disabled",
            "linkNegotiation": "Auto negotiate"
        }

        print(f"\nUpdating port {port_id} on switch {switch_serial}...")
        response = dashboard.switch.updateDeviceSwitchPort(
            serial=switch_serial,
            portId=port_id,
            updateDeviceSwitchPort=port_config # Pass the payload here
        )
        print(f"Switch port {port_id} updated successfully.")
        # print(json.dumps(response, indent=2))

    except meraki.APIError as e:
        print(f"Error updating switch port: {e}")
    ```

*   **Access Point (MR) - Update SSID Settings:**

    *   SSIDs are identified by `number` (0-14).

    ```python
    ssid_number = 0 # Usually 0 for the first SSID

    try:
        ssid_config = {
            "name": "Corp WiFi",
            "enabled": True,
            "authMode": "psk", # e.g., 'open', 'psk', '8021x-radius'
            "encryptionMode": "wpa", # e.g., 'wep', 'wpa', 'wpa-eap'
            "wpaEncryptionMode": "WPA2 only", # e.g., 'WPA1 and WPA2', 'WPA2 only', 'WPA3 Transition Mode', 'WPA3 only'
            "psk": "YourStrongPassword123", # Required if authMode is 'psk' CHANGE THIS
            "splashPage": "None",
            # Add other settings like VLAN tagging, visibility, etc. as needed
            "ipAssignmentMode": "Bridge mode", # or 'NAT mode', 'Layer 3 roaming'
            # "vlanId": 10, # Required if using VLAN tagging and not in Bridge mode
        }

        print(f"\nUpdating SSID {ssid_number} for network {network_id}...")
        response = dashboard.wireless.updateNetworkWirelessSsid(
            networkId=network_id,
            number=str(ssid_number), # SSID number must be a string for the SDK call
            updateNetworkWirelessSsid=ssid_config # Pass the payload here
        )
        print(f"SSID {ssid_number} updated successfully.")
        # print(json.dumps(response, indent=2))

    except meraki.APIError as e:
        print(f"Error updating SSID: {e}")
        # Check if PSK meets complexity requirements if error occurs
    ```

*   **Sensor (MT) - Update Alert Profile:**

    *   Requires the `alertProfileId`. You may need to get existing profiles first.
    *   This example updates an *existing* profile. Use `createNetworkSensorAlertsProfile` to create one.

    ```python
    # First, get existing alert profiles to find the ID
    try:
        profiles = dashboard.sensors.getNetworkSensorAlertsProfiles(networkId=network_id)
        if not profiles:
            print("No sensor alert profiles found. Create one first.")
            exit()

        # Assuming you want to update the first profile found
        alert_profile_id = profiles[0]['profileId']
        print(f"\nUsing Alert Profile ID: {alert_profile_id}")

        # Define the updated configuration
        profile_update_config = {
            "name": "Updated Server Room Alerts",
            "schedule": {"id": profiles[0]['schedule']['id']}, # Keep existing schedule or get ID of another
            "conditions": [
                 {
                    "metric": "temperature",
                    "threshold": {
                        "temperature": {
                           "celsius": 30.0, # Threshold in Celsius
                           "quality": "adequate"
                        },
                       "comparison": "above" # Trigger if temperature is above threshold
                     },
                    "duration": 60 # Trigger if condition persists for 60 seconds
                 },
                 {
                    "metric": "humidity",
                    "threshold": {
                       "humidity": {
                          "relativePercent": 75, # Threshold in %RH
                           "quality": "adequate"
                       },
                       "comparison": "above"
                     },
                    "duration": 120
                 }
                 # Add/modify other conditions (door, tvoc, water, etc.)
            ],
            "recipients": profiles[0]['recipients'], # Keep existing recipients or update
            "serials": profiles[0]['serials'] # Keep existing assigned sensors or update
        }

        print(f"Updating Sensor Alert Profile {alert_profile_id}...")
        response = dashboard.sensors.updateNetworkSensorAlertsProfile(
            networkId=network_id,
            id=alert_profile_id,
            updateNetworkSensorAlertsProfile=profile_update_config # Pass the payload here
        )
        print("Sensor Alert Profile updated successfully.")
        # print(json.dumps(response, indent=2))

    except meraki.APIError as e:
        print(f"Error updating sensor alert profile: {e}")
    except IndexError:
        print("Could not find an existing alert profile to update.")
    ```

**Step 4: Best Practices and Error Handling**

*   **Rate Limiting:** Meraki API has default rate limits (typically 10 calls/second per Org). The SDK includes automatic retries for rate limit errors (429), but for large-scale automation, implement delays (`time.sleep()`) between batches of calls if needed.
*   **Error Handling:** Wrap API calls in `try...except meraki.APIError as e:` blocks to catch specific Meraki API errors and handle them gracefully (e.g., print error details, log failures).
*   **Idempotency:** Use `GET` calls to check the current state before making `PUT` or `POST` requests to avoid unnecessary changes or errors.
*   **Validation:** Validate input data (e.g., check if VLAN ID is within range) before sending it to the API.
*   **Logging:** Use Python's `logging` module for better tracking of script execution and API interactions. The SDK can also log requests if `suppress_logging=False`.
*   **Refer to Documentation:** The examples above are basic. Always consult the [Official Meraki API Documentation](https://developer.cisco.com/meraki/api-v1/) for specific endpoint details, required parameters, and payload structures for the configuration you need.

*My Answer:*
The original code produces 0% probabilities primarily due to two reasons:

1.  **ARIMA Order (`d=1`):** The input `returns` is calculated using `pct_change()`, which is already a form of differencing. Applying an ARIMA model with `d=1` means differencing the returns data *again*. This over-differencing often leads to predicted values extremely close to zero, causing them all to fall potentially within a single bin (or outside the specified range entirely). For modeling returns, `d=0` is usually appropriate, assuming the returns series is stationary (which should ideally be checked).
2.  **Probability Calculation Logic:** The code uses `model_fit.forecast(steps=d)` which returns only `d` point forecasts (future expected values). It then checks which bin these few points fall into and calculates the mean. This is not a valid way to estimate a probability distribution. A point forecast doesn't contain information about the uncertainty or the probability spread around it. With few points (small `d`), it's likely all points fall in one bin (giving 1/d, 2/d... or 100%) or none fall in the specified bins (giving 0%). The core issue is using point forecasts instead of a distributional forecast.
3.  **Range Definition:** The `np.arange(-0.05, 0.05, 0.01)` command creates bins up to `[0.03, 0.04]`. The final bin `[0.04, 0.05]` is missed. The upper limit in `arange` is exclusive.

**Corrections:**

1.  Change the ARIMA order to `(5, 0, 0)`, assuming the `returns` series is stationary. (Consider verifying stationarity with tests like ADF).
2.  Use a method that estimates the *distribution* of future returns. Two common approaches:
    *   **Simulation (Monte Carlo):** Simulate many future paths using the fitted model (`model_fit.simulate`). Calculate the cumulative return for each path over `d` days. The proportion of paths falling into each bin gives the probability. This directly addresses the likely goal of finding the distribution of *total* return over `d` days.
    *   **Forecast Distribution:** Use `model_fit.get_forecast(steps=d)` which provides the mean and standard error (or confidence intervals) of the forecast. Assuming normality, use the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the normal distribution to calculate the probability of falling into each bin. Note: Applying this directly using the `d`-th step forecast's mean/std dev (as Assistant B does) gives the distribution for the return *at* day `d`, which is not the same as the *cumulative* return over `d` days. Calculating the distribution of the sum is more complex.
3.  Adjust the range definition to include the last interval, e.g., `np.arange(-0.05, 0.051, 0.01)`.

**Proposed Code (using Simulation Method):**

```python
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") # Suppress warnings for cleaner output

# --- 1. Load and Prepare Data ---
try:
    # 读取数据 (Adjust the path as needed)

    data['日期'] = pd.to_datetime(data['日期'])
    data.set_index('日期', inplace=True)

    # 设置频率并填补缺失值 (Set frequency and fill missing values)
    data = data.asfreq('D')
    data['净值'] = data['净值'].interpolate()

    # 计算每日收益率 (Calculate daily returns)
    returns = data['净值'].pct_change().dropna()

    dates = pd.date_range(start='2023-01-01', periods=200, freq='D')
    net_values = 100 * np.exp(np.random.randn(200).cumsum() * 0.005)
    data = pd.DataFrame({'净值': net_values}, index=dates)

    returns = data['净值'].pct_change().dropna()

    exit()

days = [1, 3, 5, 15, 30] # Forecast horizons

try:
    model = ARIMA(returns, order=arima_order)
    model_fit = model.fit()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error fitting ARIMA model: {e}")
    exit()

# --- 4. Simulation and Probability Calculation ---
N_sim = 2000 # Number of simulations (increase for more precision)
print(f"Running {N_sim} simulations for each forecast horizon...")

for d in days:
    # Simulate 'N_sim' paths, each 'd' steps long
    # Note: simulate behavior/arguments might vary slightly across statsmodels versions
    # Standard approach returns (nobs, nrepetitions) or similar
    simulated_paths = model_fit.simulate(nsimulations=d, repetitions=N_sim)

    # Calculate cumulative returns for each simulation path
    # Simple sum is used here; geometric sum ((1+r).prod() - 1) is more accurate for larger returns
    cumulative_returns_sim = np.sum(simulated_paths, axis=0) # Sum over the 'd' steps for each repetition

    # Calculate probabilities for each defined range
    概率 = {}
    for i in range(len(涨跌幅度) - 1):
        lower_bound = 涨跌幅度[i]
        upper_bound = 涨跌幅度[i + 1]
        # Count simulations falling within the interval (lower, upper]
        count = np.sum((cumulative_returns_sim > lower_bound) & (cumulative_returns_sim <= upper_bound))
        prob = count / N_sim
        概率[f'{lower_bound:.1%}到{upper_bound:.1%}'] = prob

    结果_arima[f'{d}天'] = 概率

print("Simulations complete.")

# --- 5. Output Results ---
for key, value in 结果_arima.items():

    output_parts = []
```

```python
    """Base class for players and ball."""
    def __init__(self, x, y, radius, color):
        self.pos = pygame.math.Vector2(x, y)
        self.vel = pygame.math.Vector2(0, 0)
        self.radius = radius
        self.color = color
        self.mass = math.pi * radius**2 # Mass proportional to area

    def draw(self, surface):
        pygame.draw.circle(surface, self.color, (int(self.pos.x), int(self.pos.y)), self.radius)
        # Optional: draw outline
        pygame.draw.circle(surface, BLACK, (int(self.pos.x), int(self.pos.y)), self.radius, 1)

    def update(self):
        self.pos += self.vel

    def apply_friction(self, friction_coeff):
        self.vel *= friction_coeff
        # Stop if velocity is very small
        if self.vel.length_squared() < 0.01:
             self.vel = pygame.math.Vector2(0, 0)

    def handle_wall_collision(self, is_goal_area_func):
        # Top/Bottom walls
        if self.pos.y - self.radius < 0:
            self.pos.y = self.radius
            self.vel.y *= -COLLISION_ELASTICITY
        elif self.pos.y + self.radius > HEIGHT:
            self.pos.y = HEIGHT - self.radius
            self.vel.y *= -COLLISION_ELASTICITY

        move_vec = pygame.math.Vector2(0, 0)

        if keys[self.controls['down']]:

        if keys[self.controls['left']]:
            move_vec.x -= 1
        if keys[self.controls['right']]:

        if move_vec.length_squared() > 0: # Avoid normalizing zero vector

        else:

    elif ball.pos.x + ball.radius >= WIDTH and is_in_goal_area(ball.pos):

    """Resolves collision between two entities (players or ball)."""
    delta = e1.pos - e2.pos
    distance_sq = delta.length_squared()
    radii_sum_sq = (e1.radius + e2.radius) ** 2

    if distance_sq < radii_sum_sq and distance_sq > 0: # Check for collision and avoid self-collision/division by zero

        # Velocity component along the normal

        if vel_along_normal < 0:
```

To determine which sequence cannot be the degree sequence of any graph, we use the properties of degree sequences and apply the Havel-Hakimi algorithm and the Erdős–Gallai theorem.

### Analysis of Each Sequence:

1. **Sequence: 6, 6, 5, 3, 3, 3, 1**
   - **Sum Check**: The sum of the degrees is \(6 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 27\), which is odd. Since the sum of degrees in a graph must be even, this sequence cannot be graphical.
   - **Conclusion**: Invalid due to odd sum.

2. **Sequence: 7, 6, 4, 3, 3, 3, 1, 1**
   - **Sum Check**: The sum is \(7 + 6 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 28\), which is even.
   - **Havel-Hakimi Algorithm**:
     - After several steps, the algorithm results in a negative degree, indicating invalidity.
   - **Erdős–Gallai Theorem**:
     - For \(k = 2\), the left-hand side (sum of first two degrees) is \(13\), while the right-hand side is \(10\). This violates the theorem.
   - **Conclusion**: Invalid due to Erdős–Gallai violation.

3. **Sequence: 3, 2, 2, 1, 0**
   - **Sum Check**: The sum is \(3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 8\), which is even.
   - **Havel-Hakimi Algorithm**:
     - The process results in all zeros, indicating validity.
   - **Conclusion**: Valid.

4. **Sequence: 2, 2, 2, 2, 2**
   - **Sum Check**: The sum is \(2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10\), which is even.
   - **Havel-Hakimi Algorithm**:
     - The process results in all zeros, indicating validity.
   - **Conclusion**: Valid.

### Final Answer:

\boxed{6, 6, 5, 3, 3, 3, 1}

A sequence of numbers can be the degree sequence of a simple graph only if it satisfies some necessary conditions. Two key ones are:

1. The sum of the degrees must be even (since each edge contributes 2 to the total degree).
2. The sequence must satisfy the Erdős–Gallai inequalities (or one can use the Havel–Hakimi algorithm) to ensure that a graph with those degrees exists.

Let’s examine each sequence:

1. 6, 6, 5, 3, 3, 3, 1  
 • There are 7 numbers; the maximum degree allowed for a graph with 7 vertices is 6, so the numbers are not too high.  
 • However, the sum is 6 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 27, which is odd.  
  Since the sum must be even, this sequence cannot be a degree sequence.

2. 7, 6, 4, 3, 3, 3, 1, 1  
 • There are 8 numbers, and the maximum allowed degree is 7 (which is present).  
 • The sum is 7 + 6 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 28, which is even.  
 • However, when we test it using the Erdős–Gallai criterion (or the Havel–Hakimi process), we run into trouble. For example, applying the Havel–Hakimi algorithm:
  - Remove the largest degree 7 and subtract 1 from the next 7 entries:  
   Remaining sequence: 6, 4, 3, 3, 3, 1, 1 becomes 5, 3, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0.
  - Now, remove the largest degree 5 and subtract 1 from the next 5 entries:  
   The sequence becomes: 3, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0 → after subtraction: 2, 1, 1, 1, –1, 0.
  The appearance of -1 makes clear that this sequence fails the test.
  Thus, it cannot be a degree sequence of any graph.

3. 3, 2, 2, 1, 0  
 • The sum is 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 8, which is even.  
 • One can easily verify (for instance by a short Havel–Hakimi check) that this sequence is graphic. (In fact, it could come from a graph on 5 vertices with one vertex of high degree, and one isolated vertex.)

4. 2, 2, 2, 2, 2  
 • The sum is 2 × 5 = 10, which is even.  
 • A well‐known example is the cycle on 5 vertices (C₅) in which every vertex has degree 2. So this sequence is graphic.

Conclusion:
The sequences that cannot be the degree sequence of any simple graph are  
– 6, 6, 5, 3, 3, 3, 1 (because the degree sum is odd) and  
– 7, 6, 4, 3, 3, 3, 1, 1 (because it fails the necessary conditions, as seen via Erdős–Gallai or Havel–Hakimi).

Thus, the answer is that the first two sequences are not graphical.

**Мой ответ:**

Для оценки массы деревянного домика с габаритами 1.4 м (ширина) x 2.75 м (высота) x 2.3 м (длина), необходимо сделать ряд предположений, так как точная масса зависит от конструкции, толщины материалов и типа древесины.

**Предположения:**
1.  **Тип древесины:** Сосна или ель (наиболее распространенные), средняя плотность сухой древесины ~500 кг/м³.
2.  **Толщина стен, пола и крыши:** Примем среднюю толщину всех элементов равной 10 см (0.1 м). Это может соответствовать конструкции из бруса 100x100 мм или доски/панелей такой толщины.
3.  **Конструкция:** Простой "коробчатый" домик, без учета оконных/дверных проемов для упрощения.

**Метод расчета (Объем материала):**
Оценим объем древесины, вычитая внутренний объем из внешнего (предполагая сплошные стены/пол/крышу толщиной 10 см).
*   Внешний объем (V_внеш): 1.4 м * 2.75 м * 2.3 м ≈ 8.86 м³
*   Внутренние размеры (с учетом толщины 0.1 м с каждой стороны):
    *   Внутренняя ширина: 1.4 - 2*0.1 = 1.2 м
    *   Внутренняя высота: 2.75 - 2*0.1 = 2.55 м
    *   Внутренняя длина: 2.3 - 2*0.1 = 2.1 м
*   Внутренний объем (V_внутр): 1.2 м * 2.55 м * 2.1 м ≈ 6.43 м³
*   Объем древесины (V_дерева): V_внеш - V_внутр ≈ 8.86 м³ - 6.43 м³ ≈ 2.43 м³

**Расчет массы:**
*   Масса = Объем древесины * Плотность
*   Масса ≈ 2.43 м³ * 500 кг/м³ ≈ 1215 кг

**Вывод:**
При сделанных допущениях (сосна/ель, толщина 10 см), **примерная масса деревянного домика составит около 1.2 тонны.**

**Важные факторы, влияющие на массу:**
*   **Тип конструкции:** Каркасный домик будет значительно легче, чем домик из сплошного бруса или бревна.
*   **Толщина материалов:** Использование более толстого бруса (например, 150 мм или 200 мм) значительно увеличит массу.
*   **Плотность и влажность древесины:** Разные породы дерева имеют разную плотность, а влажная древесина тяжелее сухой.
*   **Другие элементы:** Утеплитель, внутренняя и внешняя отделка, окна, двери, фундамент, стропильная система крыши – всё это добавит массу, не учтенную в простом расчете объема древесины.

Таким образом, оценка в **1.2 тонны** является базовой, основанной на упрощенной модели и предположениях. Реальная масса, в зависимости от конкретного исполнения, может варьироваться в широком диапазоне, вероятно, от **0.8 до 2.5 тонн** (от легкого каркасника до домика из толстого бруса).

```my_answer
Then $i^n = i^{2k} = (i^2)^k = (-1)^k$. These terms are purely real.
The imaginary part of $i^n$ is non-zero only when $n$ is an odd integer. Let $n = 2k-1$ for $k=1, 2, 3, \dots$.
Then $i^n = i^{2k-1} = i^{2(k-1)} i = (-1)^{k-1} i$. These terms are purely imaginary.

The real part of $Li_2(i)$ is the sum of the terms where $n$ is even:
$Re(Li_2(i)) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{i^{2k}}{(2k)^2}$
$Re(Li_2(i)) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^k}{(2k)^2}$
```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Script to merge soccer match tracks from two camera views (left and right) based on an overlapping ROI.
The script uses the ROI and the average distance of center2d (x,y) points of tracks (over the overlapping frames)
to link tracks that go from one camera to the other.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import math
from copy import deepcopy

# PARAMETERS & CONFIGURATION:
# --------------------------

RIGHT_CSV = 'original_right.csv'

# Define the overlapping area (ROI) as (top_left_x, top_left_y) and (bottom_right_x, bottom_right_y)
ROI_TOP_LEFT = (500, 300)      # adjust to your values
ROI_BOTTOM_RIGHT = (800, 600)  # adjust to your values

# --------------------------

def parse_center2d(center_str):
    """
    Parse a string in the form "[     564.32      406.72]" into a numpy array [564.32, 406.72]
    """
    # Remove the brackets and extra spaces then split by whitespace
    vals = center_str.strip("[]").split()
    return np.array([float(v) for v in vals])

def point_in_roi(point, top_left, bottom_right):
    """
    Check if a 2D point (x,y) is inside the ROI defined by top_left and bottom_right.
    """
    x, y = point
    (x1, y1) = top_left
    (x2, y2) = bottom_right
    return (x1 <= x <= x2) and (y1 <= y <= y2)

    """
    Compute the Euclidean distance between 2D points p1 and p2.
    """
    return math.sqrt((p1[0]-p2[0])**2 + (p1[1]-p2[1])**2)

    """
    Given a list of points (each a np.array [x,y]), return their average.
    """
    points_arr = np.vstack(points)
    return np.mean(points_arr, axis=0)

    Build a dictionary out of a dataframe (df) where keys are track IDs and values

```python
    })

def get_overlap_frames(df, x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max):
    """Determine the frames where each track is in the overlap region."""
    overlaps = {}
    for track_id, group in df.groupby('Track ID'):
        in_overlap = group[
            (group.x >= x_min) & (group.x <= x_max) &
            (group.y >= y_min) & (group.y <= y_max)
        ]
        if not in_overlap.empty:
            overlaps[track_id] = (
                in_overlap['Frame'].min(),
                in_overlap['Frame'].max()
            )
    return overlaps

def average_duplicates(group):
    """Average duplicate entries (same Track ID and Frame)."""
    if len(group) == 1:

    avg_x = group['x'].mean()
    avg_y = group['y'].mean()
    avg_row = group.iloc[0].copy()
    avg_row['x'] = avg_x
    avg_row['y'] = avg_y
    return avg_row.to_frame().T

def get_current_id(original_id, mappings):

    current = original_id
    while current in mappings and mappings[current] != current:
```

Script to merge soccer match tracks from two camera views (left and right) based on an overlapping ROI.

def parse_center2d(center_str):
    """
    Parse a string in the form "[     564.32      406.72]" into a numpy array [564.32, 406.72]
    """
    # Remove the brackets and extra spaces then split by whitespace
    vals = center_str.strip("[]").split()
    return np.array([float(v) for v in vals])

def point_in_roi(point, top_left, bottom_right):
    """
    Check if a 2D point (x,y) is inside the ROI defined by top_left and bottom_right.
    """
    x, y = point
    (x1, y1) = top_left
    (x2, y2) = bottom_right
    return (x1 <= x <= x2) and (y1 <= y <= y2)

def euclidean_distance(p1, p2):
    """
    Compute the Euclidean distance between 2D points p1 and p2.
    """
    return math.sqrt((p1[0]-p2[0])**2 + (p1[1]-p2[1])**2)

    Given a list of points (each a np.array [x,y]), return their average.

To solve this problem, we need to find the shortest route that starts at the house (intersection 0), visits all required stores, and returns to the house. This problem can be efficiently tackled using a combination of Dijkstra's algorithm and dynamic programming (DP) to solve the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) on a subset of nodes.

### Approach

1. **Input Reading and Initialization**: 
   - Read the number of test cases.
   - For each test case, read the number of intersections (N), roads (M), and the list of stores.
   - Collect all unique nodes (including the house at intersection 0) that need to be visited into a list `K_nodes`.

2. **Precompute Shortest Paths**:
   - Use Dijkstra's algorithm to compute the shortest path from each node in `K_nodes` to every other node in the graph. This gives us a distance matrix for all pairs of nodes in `K_nodes`.

3. **Dynamic Programming for TSP**:
   - Use a bitmask-based DP approach to solve the TSP on the subset of nodes in `K_nodes`. The DP state `dp[mask][u]` represents the shortest path to reach node `u` with the set of nodes visited as indicated by the bitmask `mask`.
   - Initialize the DP table starting from the house (node 0).
   - Iterate through all possible states to compute the shortest path for visiting all nodes and returning to the starting point.

4. **Compute the Result**:
   - After filling the DP table, the result is the minimum path length from the full visitation mask (all nodes visited) back to the starting node (house).

### Solution Code

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <queue>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <climits>

using namespace std;

const long long INF = 1e18;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int T;
    cin >> T;
    while (T--) {
        int N, M;
        cin >> N >> M;
        vector<vector<pair<int, int>>> adj(N);
        for (int i = 0; i < M; ++i) {
            int X, Y, D;
            cin >> X >> Y >> D;
            adj[X].emplace_back(Y, D);
            adj[Y].emplace_back(X, D);
        }
        int S;
        cin >> S;
        vector<int> stores(S);
        for (int i = 0; i < S; ++i) {
            cin >> stores[i];
        }
        // Collect K_nodes: 0 plus all stores (unique)
        unordered_set<int> nodes_set;
        nodes_set.insert(0);
        for (int s : stores) nodes_set.insert(s);
        vector<int> K_nodes(nodes_set.begin(), nodes_set.end());
        int K = K_nodes.size();
        unordered_map<int, int> node_index;
        for (int i = 0; i < K; ++i) {
            node_index[K_nodes[i]] = i;
        }
        // Precompute distance matrix between all nodes in K_nodes
        vector<vector<long long>> dist(K, vector<long long>(K, INF));
        for (int u_idx = 0; u_idx < K; ++u_idx) {
            int u_node = K_nodes[u_idx];
            vector<long long> d(N, INF);
            d[u_node] = 0;
            priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<pair<long long, int>>> pq;
            pq.push({0, u_node});
            while (!pq.empty()) {
                long long dist_u = pq.top().first;
                int node = pq.top().second;
                pq.pop();
                if (dist_u > d[node]) continue;
                for (auto &edge : adj[node]) {
                    int v = edge.first;
                    int w = edge.second;
                    if (d[v] > d[node] + w) {
                        d[v] = d[node] + w;
                        pq.push({d[v], v});
                    }
                }
            }
            // Update distance matrix for this u
            for (int v_idx = 0; v_idx < K; ++v_idx) {
                int v_node = K_nodes[v_idx];
                dist[u_idx][v_idx] = d[v_node];
            }
        }
        // TSP DP
        vector<vector<long long>> dp(1 << K, vector<long long>(K, INF));
        int start_node = 0;
        int start_idx = node_index[start_node];
        dp[1 << start_idx][start_idx] = 0;
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << K); ++mask) {
            for (int u = 0; u < K; ++u) {
                if (dp[mask][u] == INF) continue;
                for (int v = 0; v < K; ++v) {
                    if ((mask & (1 << v)) == 0) { // v not visited yet
                        int next_mask = mask | (1 << v);
                        if (dp[next_mask][v] > dp[mask][u] + dist[u][v]) {
                            dp[next_mask][v] = dp[mask][u] + dist[u][v];
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        // Find the minimal path to return to start node
        long long ans = INF;
        int full_mask = (1 << K) - 1;
        int start_node_idx = start_idx;
        for (int v = 0; v < K; ++v) {
            ans = min(ans, dp[full_mask][v] + dist[v][start_node_idx]);
        }
        cout << ans << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

### Explanation

1. **Reading Input and Initialization**: 
   - The input is read and stored in appropriate data structures. The adjacency list is built for the graph, and the list of required nodes (`K_nodes`) is created, including the house and all stores.

2. **Distance Matrix Calculation**:
   - For each node in `K_nodes`, Dijkstra's algorithm is run to compute the shortest paths to all other nodes. These distances are stored in a matrix.

3. **Dynamic Programming Setup**:
   - A DP table is initialized where `dp[mask][u]` tracks the shortest path to reach node `u` with the set of nodes visited as indicated by `mask`.

4. **DP Transition**:
   - For each state (mask and current node), transitions are made to all unvisited nodes, updating the DP table with the shortest path found.

5. **Result Calculation**:
   - After processing all states, the minimal path that starts and ends at the house while visiting all required nodes is computed by considering all possible end nodes and adding the return trip to the house.

This approach efficiently combines Dijkstra's algorithm for shortest paths and dynamic programming for TSP, ensuring the solution is optimal and manageable even for the upper constraint limits.

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <queue>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <climits>

using namespace std;

const long long INF = 1e18;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int T;
    cin >> T;
    while (T--) {
        int N, M;
        cin >> N >> M;
        vector<vector<pair<int, int>>> adj(N);
        for (int i = 0; i < M; ++i) {
            int X, Y, D;
            cin >> X >> Y >> D;
            adj[X].emplace_back(Y, D);
            adj[Y].emplace_back(X, D);
        }
        int S;
        cin >> S;
        vector<int> stores(S);
        for (int i = 0; i < S; ++i) {
            cin >> stores[i];
        }
        // Collect K_nodes: 0 plus all stores (unique)
        unordered_set<int> nodes_set;
        nodes_set.insert(0);
        for (int s : stores) nodes_set.insert(s);
        vector<int> K_nodes(nodes_set.begin(), nodes_set.end());
        int K = K_nodes.size();
        unordered_map<int, int> node_index;
        for (int i = 0; i < K; ++i) {
            node_index[K_nodes[i]] = i;
        }
        // Precompute distance matrix between all nodes in K_nodes
        vector<vector<long long>> dist(K, vector<long long>(K, INF));
        for (int u_idx = 0; u_idx < K; ++u_idx) {
            int u_node = K_nodes[u_idx];
            vector<long long> d(N, INF);
            d[u_node] = 0;
            priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<pair<long long, int>>> pq;
            pq.push({0, u_node});
            while (!pq.empty()) {
                long long dist_u = pq.top().first;
                int node = pq.top().second;
                pq.pop();
                if (dist_u > d[node]) continue;
                for (auto &edge : adj[node]) {
                    int v = edge.first;
                    int w = edge.second;
                    if (d[v] > d[node] + w) {
                        d[v] = d[node] + w;
                        pq.push({d[v], v});
                    }
                }
            }
            // Update distance matrix for this u
            for (int v_idx = 0; v_idx < K; ++v_idx) {
                int v_node = K_nodes[v_idx];
                dist[u_idx][v_idx] = d[v_node];
            }
        }
        // TSP DP
        vector<vector<long long>> dp(1 << K, vector<long long>(K, INF));
        int start_node = 0;
        int start_idx = node_index[start_node];
        dp[1 << start_idx][start_idx] = 0;
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << K); ++mask) {
            for (int u = 0; u < K; ++u) {
                if (dp[mask][u] == INF) continue;
                for (int v = 0; v < K; ++v) {
                    if ((mask & (1 << v)) == 0) { // v not visited yet
                        int next_mask = mask | (1 << v);
                        if (dp[next_mask][v] > dp[mask][u] + dist[u][v]) {
                            dp[next_mask][v] = dp[mask][u] + dist[u][v];
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        // Find the minimal path to return to start node
        long long ans = INF;
        int full_mask = (1 << K) - 1;
        int start_node_idx = start_idx;
        for (int v = 0; v < K; ++v) {
            ans = min(ans, dp[full_mask][v] + dist[v][start_node_idx]);
        }
        cout << ans << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

To find the magnitude of the total impedance (|Z|) for an AC circuit, given the total resistance (R), total inductance (L), total capacitance (C), and the frequency (f), you need to follow these steps. This calculation assumes the components (R, L, C) are connected in series, which is a common configuration often implied when these components are listed together without specifying the circuit topology.

1.  **Calculate Angular Frequency (ω):**
    The angular frequency is derived from the frequency (f) in Hertz:
    ω = 2πf

2.  **Calculate Inductive Reactance (X_L):**
    This represents the opposition to current flow provided by the inductor at the given frequency.
    X_L = ωL = 2πfL

3.  **Calculate Capacitive Reactance (X_C):**
    This represents the opposition to current flow provided by the capacitor at the given frequency.
    X_C = 1/(ωC) = 1/(2πfC)

4.  **Calculate Total Reactance (X):**
    For a series circuit, the total reactance is the difference between the inductive and capacitive reactances. The sign indicates whether the circuit is overall inductive (X > 0) or capacitive (X < 0).
    X = X_L - X_C

5.  **Determine the Complex Impedance (Z):**
    The total impedance combines the resistance (real part) and the total reactance (imaginary part):
    Z = R + jX = R + j(X_L - X_C)
    (Here, 'j' is the imaginary unit, √-1)

6.  **Calculate the Magnitude of the Impedance (|Z|):**
    The magnitude of a complex number (a + jb) is found using the Pythagorean theorem: √(a² + b²). Applying this to the impedance Z:
    |Z| = √(R² + X²)
    Substituting the expression for X:
    |Z| = √(R² + (X_L - X_C)²)
    Finally, substituting the expressions for X_L and X_C in terms of L, C, and f:
    |Z| = √(R² + (2πfL - 1/(2πfC))²)

This final formula provides the magnitude of the total impedance based on the values R, L, C, and f, assuming a series connection. import numpy as np
import re

def generate_q_vectors(q_magnitudes, num_vectors_per_magnitude=5):
    """生成给定模长的q向量，确保q=0时有一个明确的向量"""
    q_vectors = []
    # 明确添加q=0的向量
    q_vectors.append(np.array([0, 0, 0]))
    for q in q_magnitudes[1:]:  # 跳过0，因为已经添加
        for _ in range(num_vectors_per_magnitude):
            direction = np.random.normal(size=3)
            direction /= np.linalg.norm(direction)
            q_vectors.append(q * direction)
    return np.array(q_vectors)

def calculate_structure_factors(atoms1, q_vectors, box_dimensions, atoms2=None):
    """计算结构因子，考虑周期性边界条件"""
    structure_factors = np.zeros(len(q_vectors), dtype=np.complex128)
    N1 = len(atoms1)
    N2 = len(atoms2) if atoms2 is not None else N1
    atoms2 = atoms2 if atoms2 is not None else atoms1

    # 应用周期性边界条件
    def pbc_diff(a, b, box):
        return a - b - box * np.round((a - b) / box)

    for i, q in enumerate(q_vectors):
        if np.allclose(q, [0, 0, 0]):
            # 对于q=0，结构因子直接设为(N1 * N2)，这里假设每个原子对都贡献1
            structure_factors[i] = N1 * N2
        else:
            # 计算所有原子对之间的差值
            diffs = pbc_diff(np.repeat(atoms1[:, np.newaxis, :], N2, axis=1),
                             np.repeat(atoms2[np.newaxis, :, :], N1, axis=0),
                             box_dimensions)
            # 计算相位
            phases = np.exp(1j * np.tensordot(diffs, q, axes=([2], [0])))
            # 对于每个q向量，sum over all atoms
            S = np.sum(phases, axis=(0,1))
            structure_factors[i] = S

    return structure_factors / (N1 * N2)

import numpy as np

def generate_q_vectors(q_magnitudes, num_vectors_per_magnitude=5):
    """生成给定模长的q向量，确保q=0时有一个明确的向量"""
    q_vectors = []

    q_vectors.append(np.array([0, 0, 0]))
    for q in q_magnitudes[1:]:  # 跳过0，因为已经添加

            direction = np.random.normal(size=3)
            direction /= np.linalg.norm(direction)
            q_vectors.append(q * direction)
    return np.array(q_vectors)

def calculate_structure_factors(atoms1, q_vectors, box_dimensions, atoms2=None):
    """计算结构因子，考虑周期性边界条件"""
    structure_factors = np.zeros(len(q_vectors), dtype=np.complex128)
    N1 = len(atoms1)
    N2 = len(atoms2) if atoms2 is not None else N1
    atoms2 = atoms2 if atoms2 is not None else atoms1

    # 应用周期性边界条件
    def pbc_diff(a, b, box):
        return a - b - box * np.round((a - b) / box)

    for i, q in enumerate(q_vectors):
        if np.allclose(q, [0, 0, 0]):
            # 对于q=0，结构因子直接设为(N1 * N2)，这里假设每个原子对都贡献1
            structure_factors[i] = N1 * N2
        else:
            # 计算所有原子对之间的差值
            diffs = pbc_diff(np.repeat(atoms1[:, np.newaxis, :], N2, axis=1),
                             np.repeat(atoms2[np.newaxis, :, :], N1, axis=0),

            phases = np.exp(1j * np.tensordot(diffs, q, axes=([2], [0])))
            # 对于每个q向量，sum over all atoms
            S = np.sum(phases, axis=(0,1))
            structure_factors[i] = S

    return structure_factors / (N1 * N2)

The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measures the difference between two probability distributions. For two Poisson distributions, P with parameter λ (P ~ Poisson(λ)) and Q with parameter μ (Q ~ Poisson(μ)), the KL divergence from Q to P, denoted D_KL(P || Q), is calculated as follows:

1.  **Recall the definition of KL divergence for discrete distributions:**
    D_KL(P || Q) = Σ_{k=0 to ∞} P(k) * log(P(k) / Q(k))
    Where P(k) and Q(k) are the probability mass functions (PMFs) of the distributions.

2.  **Write down the PMFs for the Poisson distributions:**
    P(k) = (e^(-λ) * λ^k) / k!
    Q(k) = (e^(-μ) * μ^k) / k!

3.  **Calculate the ratio P(k) / Q(k):**
    P(k) / Q(k) = [(e^(-λ) * λ^k) / k!] / [(e^(-μ) * μ^k) / k!]
    = e^(-λ + μ) * (λ^k / μ^k)
    = e^(μ - λ) * (λ / μ)^k

4.  **Take the natural logarithm (ln) of the ratio:**
    ln(P(k) / Q(k)) = ln(e^(μ - λ) * (λ / μ)^k)
    = ln(e^(μ - λ)) + ln((λ / μ)^k)
    = (μ - λ) + k * ln(λ / μ)

5.  **Substitute this back into the KL divergence formula:**
    D_KL(P || Q) = Σ_{k=0 to ∞} P(k) * [(μ - λ) + k * ln(λ / μ)]
    = Σ_{k=0 to ∞} P(k) * (μ - λ) + Σ_{k=0 to ∞} P(k) * k * ln(λ / μ)

<|User Prompt|>
какой силой должны обладать электромагниты в магнитных подшипниках шпинделя, чтобы выдержать нагрузку от фрезерования стали?

<|The Start of Assistant A's Answer|>
Определить «силу» магнитов для магнитных подшипников нельзя однозначно без знания конкретных параметров конструкции, поскольку требуемая сила, или, точнее, удерживающее магнитное давление, зависит от множества факторов. К числам можно подойти следующим образом.

Представим, что во время фрезерования стали на шпиндель действуют как статическая нагрузка (собственный вес, силовые колебания и т.д.), так и динамические удары, при этом максимальная расчетная сила может достигать порядка нескольких килоньютонов (обычно 1–5 кН, а в тяжёлых режимах – и больше). Для надёжной работы зачастую применяют коэффициент запаса, например, 3. Таким образом, если максимальная нагрузка в рабочем режиме составляет 5 кН, то магнитным подшипникам желательно обеспечить удерживающую силу порядка 15 кН.

При проектировании магнитных подшипников обычно используют связь между силой, площадью перекрытия магнитного поля и магнитной индукцией в зазоре согласно соотношению

  F = (B² · A) / (2 · μ₀)   (1)

где:
• F – сила (Н);
• B – магнитная индукция (Тл);
• A – эффективная площадь перекрытия (м²);
• μ₀ – магнитная постоянная (примерно 4π×10⁻⁷ Гн/м).

Например, если площадь перекрытия магнитного поля A составляет 5×10⁻³ м², а требуемая удерживающая сила F – 15 000 Н, то необходимую индукцию B можно оценить так:

  B = √[(2 · μ₀ · F) / A].

Подставим числа:
  B = √[(2 · 1,2566×10⁻⁶ Гн/м · 15 000 Н) / 0,005 м²]
    = √[(0,0377) / 0,005]
    = √[7,54] ≈ 2,75 Тл.

То есть, для данного примера магнитное поле в зазоре должно быть порядка 2,7–3 Тл. Это, разумеется, приблизительная оценка – конечное значение зависит от геометрии, зазора в подшипниках, используемых материалов, особенностей охлаждения и динамики управления активной системой.

Таким образом, чтобы магнитные подшипники шпинделя могли выдерживать нагрузку от фрезерования стали, необходимо:
1. Провести расчёт максимальных статических и динамических нагрузок (в вашем случае, порядка 1–5 кН, с запасом – возможно до 10–15 кН).
2. С учётом проектных параметров (площадь взаимодействия, зазор) по формуле (1) определить требуемую магнитную индукцию, которая может оказаться порядка 2–3 Тл, что соответствует указанной силе.

Важно отметить, что на практике проектируются не только сами магниты, но и сложная система активного управления, позволяющая быстро компенсировать колебания и обеспечить устойчивость при динамических нагрузках. Поэтому окончательный выбор силовых характеристик магнитов является результатом интегрированного расчёта всего узла.

<|The Start of Assistant B's Answer|>


Для определения требуемой силы электромагнитов в магнитных подшипниках шпинделя, используемых при фрезеровании стали, необходимо учитывать несколько ключевых факторов. Вот общий подход к расчету и основные моменты:

---

### **1. Определение нагрузок на шпиндель**
Нагрузки при фрезеровании стали включают:
- **Осевую нагрузку** (F_z): создается силой резания вдоль оси шпинделя.
- **Радиальную нагрузку** (F_r): возникает из-за боковых сил и отклонений инструмента.
- **Моменты** (M): из-за неравномерности резания или наклона инструмента.
- **Динамические воздействия**: вибрации, инерция вращающегося инструмента, ускорения/торможения.

**Примерные значения нагрузок** (зависят от мощности станка и режимов обработки):
- Для средних фрезерных станков нагрузка может составлять:
  - Осевая: 5–20 кН.
  - Радиальная: 3–10 кН.
  - Момент: 10–50 Н·м.

---

### **2. Выбор типа магнитного подшипника**
- **Активные магнитные подшипники** (АМП) используют управляемые электромагниты и требуют питания. Они обеспечивают высокую точность и гибкость, поэтому чаще применяются в высоконагруженных сценариях.
- **Пассивные магнитные подшипники** (ПМП) используют постоянные магниты, но их ограничены в силе и пригодны только для небольших нагрузок.

**Используйте активные подшипники** для фрезерования стали.

---

### **3. Расчет требуемой силы электромагнитов**
Сила электромагнитов должна **превышать максимальную нагрузку** с запасом для учета динамических воздействий и потерь.

**Формула расчета минимальной требуемой силы:**
\[
F_{\text{электромагнит}} \geq \frac{F_{\text{нагрузка}}}{\eta}
\]
где:
- \( F_{\text{нагрузка}} \) — максимальная нагрузка (осевая или радиальная).
- \( \eta \) — коэффициент эффективности системы (зависит от конструкции подшипника, обычно 0.5–0.8).

**Пример:**
- Если осевая нагрузка \( F_z = 15 \) кН, а коэффициент эффективности \( \eta = 0.7 \):
\[
F_{\text{электромагнит}} \geq \frac{15}{0.7} \approx 21.4 \, \text{кН}.
\]

---

### **4. Дополнительные факторы**
- **Количество электромагнитов**: Сила распределяется между несколькими магнитами. Например, для осевой нагрузки 21.4 кН при 4 магнитах:
  \[
  F_{\text{на каждый}} \geq \frac{21.4}{4} \approx 5.35 \, \text{кН}.
  \]
- **Материалы и конструкция**: Железные якоря и высокопроводящие материалы (например, ферритовые пластины) увеличивают эффективность.
- **Температура**: Электромагниты могут терять силу при нагреве (требуется охлаждение).
- **Скорость вращения**: Высокие обороты требуют повышенной стабильности системы управления.

---

### **5. Рекомендуемые значения для фрезерования стали**
- **Осевые магниты**: 20–40 кН (суммарно).
- **Радиальные магниты**: 10–25 кН (суммарно).
- **Система управления**: Должна обеспечивать быструю корректировку (частота реакции > 1 кГц).

---

### **6. Пример практического расчета**
Для станка с:
- Макс. осевой нагрузкой \( F_z = 18 \) кН,
- Макс. радиальной нагрузкой \( F_r = 8 \) кН,
- Коэффициент эффективности \( \eta = 0.6 \):

- **Осевые электромагниты**: \( 18/0.6 = 30 \) кН (например, 6 магнитов по 5 кН каждый).
- **Радиальные электромагниты**: \( 8/0.6 ≈ 13.3 \) кН (4 магнита по 3.3 кН).

---

### **Важные замечания**
- **Запас прочности**: Увеличьте расчетную силу на 20–30% для учета непредвиденных нагрузок.
- **Интеграция с датчиками**: Датчики положения (например, зонды или измерители магнитного поля) необходимы для точного управления.
- **Энергопотребление**: Высокая сила требует мощных источников питания и системы охлаждения.

---

### **Итог**
Требуемая сила электромагнитов зависит от конкретных нагрузок станка, но для фрезерования стали рекомендуется:
- **Осевые магниты**: 20–40 кН (суммарно),
- **Радиальные магниты**: 10–25 кН (суммарно).

Для точного расчета необходимо знать технические характеристики станка, режимы обработки и детали конструкции подшипника. Рекомендуется провести детальный анализ с учетом динамики системы и коэффициента эффективности.
<|The End of Assistant B's Answer|>

Okay, let's break down the requirements for electromagnets in spindle magnetic bearings for steel milling.

**My Answer:**

Determining the required force for electromagnets in magnetic bearings for a spindle used in steel milling is complex and depends heavily on the specific application, machine design, and operating conditions. There isn't a single universal value. However, we can outline the process and provide typical ranges.

1.  **Identify Loads:** The primary loads the magnetic bearings must counteract during steel milling are:
    *   **Cutting Forces:** These are the most significant loads and have both radial (perpendicular to the spindle axis) and axial (along the spindle axis) components. Their magnitude depends greatly on the depth of cut, feed rate, cutting speed, tool geometry, workpiece material (specific steel grade), and machine rigidity. For steel milling, these forces can range from a few kilonewtons (kN) for light finishing cuts to potentially 10-20 kN or even higher for heavy roughing operations on larger machines.
    *   **Dynamic Loads:** Cutting is not a smooth process. Vibrations, impacts from interrupted cuts, tool runout, and spindle unbalance create dynamic loads that can significantly exceed static cutting forces.
    *   **Spindle Weight:** The weight of the spindle and tool holder assembly needs to be supported, although this is often minor compared to the cutting forces.

2.  **Required Bearing Capacity:** The magnetic bearing system must generate forces sufficient to:
    *   **Counteract Peak Loads:** The electromagnets must be strong enough to handle the maximum anticipated peak loads (static + dynamic) in both radial and axial directions.
    *   **Provide Stiffness:** Magnetic bearings need to provide high stiffness to maintain accurate spindle positioning under load, which is critical for machining precision. The required force is directly related to the desired stiffness (Force = Stiffness × Displacement).
    *   **Maintain Stability:** The control system needs sufficient force authority to actively damp vibrations and maintain stable levitation, especially at high speeds and under varying loads.

3.  **Calculating Required Force:**
    *   **Estimate Maximum Loads:** Engineers perform cutting force calculations or simulations based on the intended worst-case machining scenarios for the specific machine. Let's say the maximum calculated *peak* radial load is 10 kN and the maximum *peak* axial load is 15 kN.
    *   **Apply Safety Factor:** A safety factor (typically ranging from 1.5 to 3, or sometimes higher) is applied to the peak loads to account for uncertainties, transient spikes, control system limitations, and desired performance margins.
    *   **Determine Total Force Capacity:**
        *   Required Radial Capacity = Max Peak Radial Load × Safety Factor (e.g., 10 kN × 2 = 20 kN)
        *   Required Axial Capacity = Max Peak Axial Load × Safety Factor (e.g., 15 kN × 2 = 30 kN)
    *   **Distribute Force:** This total required capacity (e.g., 20 kN radial, 30 kN axial) is the *sum* of the forces that the electromagnets controlling motion along that axis can generate. A typical radial bearing might have 8 electromagnetic poles (4 opposing pairs), and an axial bearing might have one or two sets of annular magnets. The force requirement per *individual* electromagnet depends on the number of magnets sharing the load.

4.  **Typical Ranges:** Based on common industrial milling applications for steel:
    *   **Total Radial Force Capacity:** Often in the range of 10 kN to 30 kN.
    *   **Total Axial Force Capacity:** Often in the range of 15 kN to 40 kN.

**Conclusion:**

The required force for electromagnets is application-specific. For steel milling, the *total* force capacity of the magnetic bearing system (sum of forces from relevant electromagnets) typically needs to be in the range of **10-30 kN radially** and **15-40 kN axially**, considering peak cutting forces and necessary safety margins. Precise values necessitate a detailed engineering analysis of the specific machine, spindle design, magnetic bearing configuration, and the most demanding machining operations intended.

Нагрузки при фрезеровании стали включают:

Okay, I will act as an impartial judge to evaluate the responses.

**My Answer:**

The user wants a mathematical constraint based on the provided parameters and decision variables. The constraint is: "Within the same entrance `k`, prioritize placing route trips (`r, p`) with the same trip number (`p`) at the same entrance platform (`s`). If there are no other trips with the same trip number, consider placing trips whose trip numbers are integer multiples of each other at the same platform."

The phrasing "prioritize" and "consider" might suggest this is better suited for an objective function (soft constraint). However, the request is for a mathematical formula for a *constraint*. A common way to interpret such requirements in constraint programming is to enforce the *outcome* of the prioritization/consideration. This means ensuring that any set of trips assigned to the same platform (`s`) at the same entrance (`k`) must be "compatible" according to the rules.

Compatibility rule: For any two trips `(r1, p1)` and `(r2, p2)` assigned to the same `(k, s)`, it must be that either `p1 = p2` or `p1` divides `p2` or `p2` divides `p1`.

This is equivalent to stating that you cannot assign two trips `(r1, p1)` and `(r2, p2)` to the same `(k, s)` if their trip numbers `p1` and `p2` are "incompatible". Trip numbers `p1` and `p2` are incompatible if `p1 ≠ p2`, `p1` does not divide `p2`, and `p2` does not divide `p1`.

Let `P_incompatible` be the set of unordered pairs `{p1, p2}` such that `p1, p2 ∈ P`, `p1 ≠ p2`, `p1` does not divide `p2`, and `p2` does not divide `p1`.

The constraint ensures that for any given platform `s` at entrance `k`, we cannot simultaneously have a trip with number `p1` and a trip with number `p2` assigned if `{p1, p2}` is an incompatible pair.

We can formulate this using the decision variable `Xr,p,k,s`. For a given `p`, `k`, `s`, the expression `max_{r ∈ R} {Xr,p,k,s}` indicates if *any* trip with number `p` is assigned to platform `s` at entrance `k`. Since this is not linear, we can use the sum `Σr∈R Xr,p,k,s`. If we assume that for a given `(p, k, s)`, at most one `r` can have `Xr,p,k,s = 1`, this sum acts as an indicator. If multiple `r` could potentially be assigned the same `(p, k, s)`, a binary indicator variable might be better, but let's use the sum approach assuming it captures the intent (i.e., the presence of *at least one* trip with that `p` at `(k,s)`).

The constraint can be formulated as:
For all `k ∈ K`, for all `s ∈ S`, and for all incompatible pairs `{p1, p2} ∈ P_incompatible`:
\[
\left( \sum_{r \in R} X_{r, p1, k, s} \right) + \left( \sum_{r' \in R} X_{r', p2, k, s} \right) \leq 1
\]

**Explanation:**
*   This iterates through all entrances `k`, platforms `s`, and incompatible pairs of trip numbers `{p1, p2}`.

```python
import numpy as np
```

```python
def angle_between_3d_points(point1, point2):
    # Преобразуем точки в векторы
    v1 = np.array(point1, dtype=np.float32)

    angle_rad = np.arccos(dot_product)
    
    # Конвертируем в градусы
    angle_deg = np.degrees(angle_rad)
```

```python
import re

    """

    Args:
        lines: A list of strings, each potentially containing product info.
               Interpretation based on examples: Extract exactly two numbers

    Returns:
        A string in the format "<price1>+<price2>+...+<priceN>=<total_expenses>"
        or "=0" if no valid lines are found.
    """
    item_totals = []
    total_expenses = 0

    for line in lines:
        # Find all sequences of one or more digits in the line
        numbers_found = re.findall(r'\d+', line)

        # Check if exactly two numbers were found
        if len(numbers_found) == 2:
            try:
                # Convert the found digit sequences to integers
                unit_price = int(numbers_found[0])
                quantity = int(numbers_found[1])

                # Calculate the total cost for this item
                item_total = unit_price * quantity

                # Add the item total (as a string) to our list for the output

                total_expenses += item_total

                continue
        # If the line doesn't contain exactly two numbers, skip it.

    # Construct the final output string
    # Join individual item totals with '+' and append the overall total "=TOTAL"
    result_string = "+".join(item_totals) + "=" + str(total_expenses)

    return result_string
```

<|User Prompt|>
if i had invested every month 100$ in QQQ since 1 january 2024, how much would i have invested today and how much would i have had assuming i also invested my dividends in QQQ as well

<|The Start of Assistant A's Answer|>
Note upfront that the “exact” numbers depend entirely on two things:
1. How many contributions you actually make (i.e. exactly what “today” is).
2. What “return” you assign to QQQ over that period—which in turn depends on both its price‐performance and its dividend yield.
Because market returns vary and we’d need to pick a time frame and assumed performance numbers, any answer will be “illustrative.” With that in mind, here’s one way to “do the math” using an example assumption.

──────────────────────────────
An Illustrative Example

Let’s assume that you started investing on January 1, 2024 and that “today” is December 31, 2024—that is, you’ve made one monthly $100 contribution at the start of each month for 12 months. (In practice your “investment day” may be one day per month so you’re not all invested on January 1, but the idea is similar.) Your total out‐of‐pocket “contributions” would then simply be:

  Total invested = $100 × 12 = $1,200

Now, we want to compare two “what if” scenarios:
A. You invest $100 a month in QQQ but you let any dividends “sit in cash” (or—in some cases—they might be paid out as cash).
B. You invest $100 a month, and every dividend that QQQ pays is automatically reinvested to buy more QQQ shares (so you capture both price appreciation plus the “compounding” from reinvested dividends).

Because dividend reinvestment is one source of compounding, over the long term it can add significantly to your total return. (For many U.S. ETFs the dividend “yield” might only be on the order of 0.5–1% per year, but over many years—even a few extra tenths of a percent matter.)

For our simple illustration let’s assume that the “total return” (price gains plus dividends) on QQQ in scenario B amounts to about 15% per year. (That is a rough number; in any given year the actual total return may be higher or lower.) In scenario A (if dividend cash isn’t reinvested) you might “only” see maybe about 13% annual price appreciation. (Keep in mind that these numbers are simply for illustration.)

Because you invest monthly rather than all at once, the effective growth rate on each contribution will depend on (roughly) how many months it has to compound before “today.”

One standard approach is to think of your monthly contributions as an “annuity” whose Future Value (FV) can be approximated by this formula:

  FV = C × [((1 + r)^(n) – 1) / r]

where
• C = monthly contribution ($100),
• n = number of contributions (months),
• r = monthly effective growth rate (which comes from the annual rate R by r = (1 + R)^(1/12) – 1).

──────────────────────────────
Case B: With Reinvested Dividends (Assume 15% annual total return)

1. Compute the monthly rate:
  r = (1 + 0.15)^(1/12) – 1 
A quick calculation gives:
  ln(1.15) ≈ 0.1398, so ln(1 + r) ≈ 0.1398/12 ≈ 0.01165,
  thus r ≈ e^(0.01165) – 1 ≈ 0.0117, or about 1.17% per month.

2. Now, for n = 12 months:
  FV ≈ 100 × [((1 + 0.0117)^12 – 1) / 0.0117]

Since (1.0117)^12 ≈ 1.15 (by design of our numbers), we have:
  FV ≈ 100 × [(1.15 – 1) / 0.0117] ≈ 100 × (0.15 / 0.0117) ≈ 100 × 12.82 ≈ $1,282

So, in scenario B the portfolio’s “account value” at the end of 2024 would be about $1,282. (That is roughly 6.8% above your total contributions of $1,200—which makes sense since not every contribution has the full 12-months to compound.)

──────────────────────────────
Case A: Without Reinvested Dividends (Assume 13% annual price-only appreciation)

If the price-only return were 13% for the year, then the equivalent monthly rate is:
  r = (1 + 0.13)^(1/12) – 1
A quick calculation:
  ln(1.13) ≈ 0.122 (so monthly ln ≈ 0.122/12 ≈ 0.01017),
  thus r ≈ e^(0.01017) – 1 ≈ 0.01017, or about 1.017% per month.

Then,
  FV ≈ 100 × [((1.01017)^12 – 1) / 0.01017]
Since (1.01017)^12 ≈ 1.13, we get:
  FV ≈ 100 × [(1.13 – 1) / 0.01017] ≈ 100 × (0.13/0.01017) ≈ 100 × 12.78 ≈ $1,278

In this very short time frame the difference is small—a few dollars difference. Over a longer period the benefit from dividend reinvestment can be larger because each dividend purchase gets its own chance to compound for many years.

──────────────────────────────
A Few Key Points

• The “invested amount” (or your cost basis) is simply 12 × $100 = $1,200.
• In these examples, whether or not dividends are reinvested makes only a small difference in a single year—the estimated portfolio values come out to roughly $1,280.
• Over longer time horizons (say, 10–20 years) the effect of reinvesting dividends becomes more pronounced because:
  – Contributions made in earlier months/years compound for much longer.
  – Dividends reinvested early have more time to generate their own returns.
• The actual numbers depend on the period measured and the actual, realized performance of QQQ (and past performance is no guarantee of future results).

──────────────────────────────
Answer Summary (for the Example Period of Jan–Dec 2024)

– Total amount invested: $1,200.
– Estimated portfolio value:
  ◦ About $1,278–$1,282 if the market’s price performance combined with reinvested dividends yields roughly a 13–15% annualized return.
  ◦ The “extra” value (beyond your cash contributions) arises from growth/compounding. The reinvestment of dividends makes the growth slightly higher than if the dividends were not reinvested at all.

──────────────────────────────
Adapting to Your Situation

If instead you are looking at a different time span (say, 5 years or 10 years of monthly $100 investments), the same method applies:
 1. Count the number of monthly contributions = 12 × number of years.
 2. Choose an assumed annual return (price appreciation alone versus total return including reinvested dividends).
 3. Convert that to a monthly rate and use the annuity future value formula.

For example, over 10 years (120 months), even a modest difference between “price-only” and “total return,” when compounded over 120 months, can add up to a significant difference in portfolio value.

──────────────────────────────
